maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last evening I was speaking on the resolution moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to institute a parliamentary investigation. I was expressing my firm conviction that at this critical time the Canadian people do not want a parliamentary committee, that what they want is immediate government action, action quite within the scope of the powers which the government possesses. I was referring to the serious coal strike which is now in progress in Alberta and British Columbia. I assert again that that strike is directly attributable to the fact that the coal miners' take-home pay has shrunk so greatly in purchasing power.
Unfortunately this is not the end. I am informed that the loggers and woodworkers of British Columbia are becoming increasingly restive and that they are contemplating new wage demands. In addition many thousands of unorganized workers all across the dominion are longing and praying for some immediate relief from the strain. I do not profess to believe for one moment that operating costs have no bearing on prices. Of course they have. When increases in wages are granted they are always followed by higher prices for the goods produced, whether it be coal, lumber or any other product. But increased wages are only one factor in increased prices. Wages never do catch up with prices in that kind of race. What I want to know is where this thing is going to end. There simply has to be a limit somewhere. By and large the Canadian people are patient and understanding. They follow the trend of national and

Prices Committee
international affairs, and they know that their government is bound to be faced at times with circumstances not of their own making and beyond their control. This is definitely not one of those peculiar circumstances. This is a situation which the government can and must correct. It has the power to do it but it seems to lack the will.
What are the Prime Minister and his cabinet afraid of? Are they afraid to admit that their decontrol policy was wrongly timed? The country believes that it was. Let the Prime Minister frankly and courageously admit that he and his ministers were in error in their estimation of the times; let him take drastic and immediate steps to rectify that error, and I can assure him that he need have no fear of the people of this country. I want to warn the Prime Minister and the government that if something is not done, and done quickly, the cry of the Canadian people for the control of their cost of living will develop into a tidal roar demanding the resignation of the government on the grounds of inefficiency and irresponsibility.
Before I take my seat I want to refer to the speech made by the Prime Minister when he introduced this resolution on Monday, February 2. I listened as carefully as I could to what he had to say, but I admit I was hampered by the bad acoustics of this chamber. Comparing this particular speech with others he has delivered in the house it seemed to me that the right hon. gentleman was altogether on the defensive. He was trying to make a bad situation look good, and personally I think he failed. Perhaps he will permit me to tell him that I think he is at his best when he is leading an attack. The particular part of his speech to which I wish to refer is to be found in Hansard, of Monday, February 2, at page 751, where he said:
Let me add this one word in conclusion. Hon. gentlemen opposite will doubtless continue to criticize, will doubtless belittle, wall doubtless question the motives of the government in respect of this matter. But what will tell in the end as to what they really believe will be seen when they show where they stand, not by their words, but by their votes on the appointment of this committee. I will venture to say that the numbers who will vote against the appointment of a committee to investigate this important question of rising prices and the cost of living will be mighty few indeed, if indeed there be any at all.
If the Prime Minister meant that in any way as a threat, or if he thinks that we of the opposition can be intimidated or dragooned into submission, let me say this. Speaking for myself, of course, after seeing amendment after amendment ruled out of order which would have made the committee acceptable to
a far greater degree than it is in its present form, I am quite prepared in my mind to vote against this resolution and I am also prepared to go before the electors of my constituency and tell them why I voted against it. I question whether the Prime Minister or any other member on the other side of the house is prepared to do that. I know what the electors of my constituency think about this question. They know the stand I take on it, and I know the stand they take, and I am content to abide by their judgment. I for one want no part in an emasculated, hog-tied committee. I shall vote against it. I can do no other and be true to my constituents and to my conscience.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was a time when I thought that almost everything that could be said on this resolution had already been said, but on analysing the speeches that have been made and after watching the attitude of the government with respect to amendments that have been moved, I have concluded that there are still a few loose ends that should be picked up and a few more facts stated.
I am very much pleased, as I think we all are, to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) so constant in his attendance in this house. During the war we recognized that there was considerable excuse for him and his colleagues being absent from the house, and we graciously excused their absence, knowing that they had important matters to attend to. The war is over, and this session has started out very well with the Prime Minister in his seat every moment of the day. We are pleased with that, but I do just have the suspicion that he is not sitting there merely for the benefit of his health.
The Prime Minister in introducing the motion said, at page 745 of Hansard'.
Today I am asking hon. members to appoint a select committee of this house to examine and report on matters pertaining to the recent rise in prices and in the increase in the cost of living.
If we had not seen the Prime Minister's name at the head of that resolution but had simply been scanning Hansard as an outside observer, we should have thought that such a statement and resolution was made by one of the leaders on the opposition side of the house, because it is the sort of thing that a leader of any opposition party would ask when an emergency arises.
Surely the government has some responsibility in respect to the rise in the cost of living. Surely the government has confidence in its own administration. But really it would
Prices Committee

appear that they have not, because they come to parliament and are now asking that a select committee of the house be brought into existence to do the work which we are certain their own administration could do.
There is really not much difference in principle between fluctuations in the prices of commodities and fluctuations in the value of the dollar. When there are fluctuations in the value of the dollar the government never thinks of coming to parliament and asking it to set up a committee to find out why the value of the dollar should fluctuate. Why do they not? They do not, needless to say. Yet when prices fluctuate-and the principle is the same as with fluctuations in the dollar, the only difference being that in the one case the figures appear on a bill and in the other on a price tag, the value of the dollar fluctuating with price fluctuations-the government asks parliament to appoint a committee to look into the reason for the fluctuations or upward trend in prices. Would any responsible government ask another body, particularly its opponents, to help them understand why the dollar had depreciated or fluctuated in value? I do not think they would.
If the government wants to know one reason for the increase in the cost of living, if it wants the light to shine in, I will say this: One reason why there is an increase in the cost of living is that government policy has been such as to permit the cost of living to rise. That may be quite a general statement, but surely when government policy in the past has permitted the cost of living to rise, the government must take some responsibility for it. The fact of the matter is that government policy has led us definitely into this condition. Government players in the ball field have not been able to bring in the home runs and keep ahead of the price score. Now the government wants a parliamentary committee set up to discover who muffed the ball. Further, Mr. Speaker, they want us to find out these facts, but they refuse to let us suggest to them the remedies that should be applied.
Who is it, anyway, who has steered our ship of state into these troubled waters? Surely somebody has done it. Who has been at the helm of the nation's business? Well, none other than the man who makes this motion.
If the government denies that government policy has led to these conditions, then surely they would have no objection to recommendations as to the action that should be taken to remedy them. A committee is to be set up. Much has been said about the work of the committee; that perhaps it w'ould be hog-tied.

Well, I do not like to say these things about parliamentary committees, but one is not here very long before he recognizes that parliamentary committees are not entirely free. A committee of this kind must not be set up to protect government policy. Let me just refer to the committee itself. I notice that it is composed of sixteen members. Out of that number eight are lawyers, two are manufacturers, two are farmers, one is an engineer, one a journalist, one a teacher, and one a preacher. I am glad the preacher is there. I have no desire to belittle the ability of these men. They are good men, and given a task to do and a free hand to do it they will attempt to do a good job; but since the government wants tc know the facts I do have to ask myself this question: can this committee secure the facts any better than the well-trained and reputable men who are already in the government administration?

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: Bureaucrats.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
We can call them bureaucrats if we wish. Sometimes I have used that w'ord, and I must confess that perhaps I have bounced it around a little bit too liberally at times; nevertheless I personally do not question the ability of some of the men that the government has in its administration. Before leaving that I should like to point out- I do not know how many hon. members have noticed this-that among the members of the proposed committee there is one minister of the crown, which is quite usual. In addition to the minister there are four parliamentary assistants. I wonder whether that was by accident or design. The warning I give is that this committee must not be set up in order to protect government policy. Let the light shine, and let the sparks fall where they will.
The government say they want to know the facts. Are we to believe that the government do not know the facts?

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
That is right; they
don't know anything.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Well, they claim to know everything else. Are we to believe that the government is not able to get all the facts that a parliamentary committee can get? I say that with the able officials that the government has in some of the departments the government can get the facts. I will go further and say this, that the government knows today more facts about the situation than a parliamentary committee could find out if it sat all year.

Prices Committee
I represent what is largely a farming constituency. Many farmers have come to me and complained because some inspector from the income tax branch has come round and wanted to know all the details of his business. Of course he is only a farmer; but what I am saying is they will track down the farmer, they will track down the person who, they think they have cause to believe, is not paying all his income tax. Is the government going to tell us that it has not already the facts concerning large corporations and institutions? If it says it has not these facts, I would almost suggest it has been remiss in its duty.
In his speech on February 2, as reported at page 747 of Hansard the Prime Minister said:
In regard to this class of social wrong I believe that if there are people today in Canada who are hoarding where they should be selling, and if there are others who are profiteering where they should be glad to do what is fair, just and reasonable in the matter of prices, such people will quickly take notice of the fact that this House of Commons has appointed a committee which can. go into any single phase of this problem and bring individuals from any part of the country to -answer for situations in which they may be involved.
I have sometimes criticized officials within government departments because I have not agreed with their policies, but it is their policies that I have not agreed with; I have never once said that deputy ministers, and deputies to deputies, and deputies to them, are inefficient. I believe the government has some very efficient men within its administration. Are hon. gentlemen opposite going to tell me that they are not efficient enough to be able to search out all the facts and find out who is the profiteer?
They say they want the light to shine in. Surely the government is close enough to a million dollar corporation to know whether they are profiteering at the expense of the people. If it is not, then it is remiss in its duty. Hon. gentlemen opposite say they want light to be shed on the situation. Since they have a preacher on the committee, perhaps he could lead the singing:
Clear the darkened windows, open wide the door;
Let the blessed light shine in.
That might be a good theme song for the committee. But thinking of theme songs, I have a pretty good one that the Prime Minister might sing. This situation is growing bigger and fatter every day, and perhaps he could sing:
I dorft -wan-t her; you can have her;
She's too fat for me.
Then the Prime Minister went on to suggest what the committee was not. He outlined
what the committee was, but he had to take great pains to tell us what the committee was not. At page 747 of Hansard he said:
Now just a word as to what this committee is not. The government has no desire or intention that the committee should be used in what might be described as a witch hunt, to see what persons, what firms, or what corporations may be brought into difficulties, or to have individuals, firms or corporations unnecessarily embarrassed by a public inquiry.
All he wants of the committee is to have it play bogey man to say "boo!" to the profiteers. The Prime Minister says in one breath that these individuals should be brought to time and exposed by a public inquiry, and in the next breath he says, "When you are exposing them don't cause them to blush." That is a riddle I would ask him to answer. As youngsters we used to ask riddles at our parties. Well, the riddle I want him to answer is this: How can you expose a profiteer without embarrassing him?

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: The $64 question.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
I believe in private enterprise, as I have said in this house a good many times. I believe that most businessmen want to do legitimate business; they want to be fair in their business. I believe that boards of trade throughout the country are brought into existence not merely to protect the interests of the businessman but for ethical purposes, to protect business in its right to do business on legitimate grounds. I am not one who is going around branding every man as a profiteer. I have never thought of the present system as being merely a profit system. It is that, but it is also a profit and loss system, and I believe the average businessman in Canada wants to do an honest business. But any who are unfair, any who are taking advantage of others are meanies, the sort the Prime Minister referred to. These mean evildoers should be exposed if they are making profits at the expense of the public. Their faces should be red, but they should be so spanked that not only their faces would be red.
I know there are huge corporations in this country and when, perhaps more or less superficially I read of their profits it does occur to me that some people, some corporations are making huge profits. I cannot help believing they are. At the same time when I begin to analyse a modern financial statement by a a huge industrial corporation, my head goes around in figures. I swim in them and I cannot swim out. I get in too deep. I doubt very much whether the average person can read intelligently and arrive at a proper conclusion in respect to all that is involved in
Prices Committee

profits, when reading the average financial statement. If that is a weakness on my part, then I shall have to admit it.
I do not know what the committee will do. They may go into all the ramifications of these statements. In the present discussion we have heard that living costs have jumped so many points; this thing has jumped so many points and something else has stepped down so many points, and all that. If you were to try to examine that and to arrive at the conclusion presented to you, your head might swim too. I do not do that.
Once upon a time I took a smattering of law when I thought I was going to be a big lawyer, but I never made the grade. I recall a certain case about which I read; I believe it was one in which Webster and Choate were concerned. Choate was examining a witness in court. A wagon wheel was brought in which was supposed to have been on a certain wagon. Experts, with all their figures, tried to prove that it was not the wheel off this particular wagon because it did not look like the other three wheels. They discussed the matter for a long time, and after Choate got through Webster got up and said, "Now, gentlemen of the jury, there is the wheel; take a good look at it". That was all, and he won his case.
I might go into all these price structures and not be able to arrive at a conclusion. When the housewife gets her husband's cheque she does not know anything about what causes the rise in the cost of living; she does not know how the corporations make out their financial statements. She goes to the grocery store, spends the cheque, and brings home her bag perhaps half filled with groceries and she says to her husband, "Husband, look at it". That is all; that is evidence enough for her.
If this committee in its work is going to expose the profiteers, this is the opportunity that is given any man who thinks there are huge profits made at the expense of the people. This is his opportunity to expose the profiteers. But is it his opportunity? I wonder. It has all the appearances of being the opportunity, but I wonder how many profiteers will be spanked. I wonder how many profiteers will go back home with red faces.
What is going to be the attitude if, when the committee has finished its work, no profiteers have been exposed? Are we then to assume that no profiteers exist? Are we then to assume that no one in Canada is taking advantage of a bad situation? These are some of the things that may give us some thought.
I am going to recommend seriously that the committee should put the first foot forward. I do not know what procedure the government has in mind. I know the government

has a majority on the committee, as it has on all committees. I know it has a minister and four parliamentary assistants on the committee. Perhaps it is all mapped out as to what should be done or what procedure should be taken. But they should put the first foot forward and take the first step before they attempt to take the last one. What is the most important thing to do in inquiring into the cost of living? It is to examine into those things that touch the small purses of the country, those things that touch the small wage earner. Man cannot live except by bread. Man's bread and butter is his first concern. The first thing the committee should attempt to do is to find the reasons for the increase in the cost of bread, milk, butter and meat. Let those things come in their proper order.
Much has been said about International Nickel, the Aluminum Company of Canada and other corporations as making huge profits. That has been brought into the picture in days gone by. Do not misunderstand me; if these men have been making huge profits at the expense of the people they should be exposed, if the committee sits all year to do it. Speaking about aluminum, I am anxious that the price of what goes into the pot should be examined before we examine the price of the pot. As I say, the committee should start first on flour, bread, butter, then meat; perhaps they will get to clothing. But I doubt Whether they will get much farther than flour and bread.
There is another thing I am going to say, Mr. Speaker, and I want an answer from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) or a responsible official from the government. There is no question in my mind that this is a move on the part of the government to shift their own responsibility to another body. They have steered the ship of state into these troubled waters and are now asking us to discover why we are there, without giving us the opportunity of telling them how to steer the ship out again. They *want to shift that responsibility to another body, and they are playing for time. I want the Prime Minister to answer this question and give us an assurance: If this committee is set up, will parliament as a whole be given the opportunity of discussing the reports of the committee, and, in discussion of these reports in the house, will it be given the opportunity of making suggestions as to what should be done? I anticipate the Prime Minister's answer, and it is one that I do not want, namely, "Well, my hon. friend knows the rules of the house. It is entirely in the hands of the committee. If they do not move concurrence in the report,

Prices Committee
we can always discuss it on the estimates." I imagine that will be his answer. Will he give us the assurance now that every time this committee reports, within twenty-four hours or forty-eight hours afterwards-whatever the rules may say-a motion for concurrence will be made? There should be no objection to that, since the committee is not making any recommendations. Will the Prime Minister give us that assurance?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
The debate is stretching out to quite a length, Mr. Speaker, and I do not expect to make a long speech this afternoon; perhaps I shall not take my full time. But there are a few observations I should like to make on the resolution and on some of the statements which have been made in the course of the debate on this resolution.
It seems to me that the issues here are simple, and that they are two in number. The first is whether there should be a parliamentary committee to examine into and report on the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living, which is paragraph (a) of the motion. Paragraphs (b) and (c) are, in a sense, subordinate to paragraph (a), because what is proposed is a fact-finding inquiry into the recent rise in the cost of living. The first point is whether it is worthwhile, whether it is advisable, to have a parliamentary committee examine into those causes. Then, assuming that a parliamentary inquiry is desirable, the second question is whether the terms of reference should be limited as they are in the resolution, or whether they should be virtually unlimited as has been proposed by various members of this house.
Perhaps I cannot answer these two questions conclusively or convincingly, but I can express my own views on them.
In the first place it seems to me that many members of the house are on record as advocating, in a situation of this kind, a parliamentary inquiry instead of an official or governmental inquiry into a matter of this importance. I remember an occasion when I was minister of finance and the wartime prices and trade board had authorized an increase to the extent of 12J per cent in the prices of agricultural implements. As soon as members could get to the house to attack me, the government and the board, they did so-and in numbers. Some thirty-five or forty speeches were made one Monday afternoon and evening attacking the wartime prices and trade board, myself and the government for this authorized increase in the price of agricultural implements.
Prices Committee

One of the most thoughtful and moderate members of the house-and I am' not speaking of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) but rather of his colleague who sits immediately behind him-used this language in regard to that incident. On that occasion the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) said this, as reported at page 897 of Hansard for April 15, 1946:
So that I sulbmit for the consideration, of the minister and the government whether it would not be possible to have some body, I do not know whether it should be the agriculture committee, the banking and commerce committee or a combination of the two if you wish, which would ask to appear before it people who are supposed to have competent opinions on these important questions, which I recognize as very difficult, and to ask also representatives of labour, of the farmers, of the manufacturers and of all the other people interested. The minister may say, "Oh, well, you would just have a kind of debate which would lead to nothing." I am not suggesting that this body could proceed to decide on this and this and this decontrol in gatling-igim fashion, but I suggest that at the present time there is a great deal of misapprehension in the public mind, and that if we are to have merely one announcement after another that this and this and this has been decontrolled, it is not the best way of trying to get across to the public mind what, it seems to me, it is so enormously important that we should get into the public mind.
And then later on he said this:
I believe the debate we have had today shows that the problem is not being met, when once there is this widespread measure of protest. I realize that the protests come from farming constituencies. I represent one myself, though it will be observed that I have not made a protest. Nevertheless I feel there are basic principles here which might well be discussed in open forum, so that the citizens of Canada might have a better understanding than they vow have of the problems and the basic principles which are to be followed in dealing with the matter.
Although I was not in the house at the time -I believe I was away-the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) reasoned in much the same way in respect of the industrial disputes which arose in Hamilton in 1946. And the hon. member for Lake Centre has gone so far along this line, that of advocating action by parliamentary committees, and hearings by such committees, that he, forsooth, advocated a while ago the summoning of deputy ministers and senior civil servants before a parliamentary committee to quiz them as to the advice they were giving their ministers. No stranger proposal was ever made in any British parliamentary institution. Nevertheless this is an indication of the fondness held by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and hon. members of the opposition for parliamentary

committees. So I say this is an occasion or a situation of sufficient importance to merit having the matter examined by a parliamentary committee.
In his speech the leader of the opposition Said, "Oh well, after all, what do parliamentary committees amount to? What do they ever accomplish?" And he names a whole group of parliamentary committees the proceedings of which, so he said, did not come to anything much. He said, "You have the machinery now. You have all the laws there that you need now."
One in particular he mentioned was that which I shall call the profiteering section of the wartime prices and trade board regulations. It is the section which provides that no person shall, in selling goods, charge a price which exceeds that which is just and reasonable. He said, "Why dio you not use that? Why does not the government use that regulation?"
During the course of the debate there has been considerable reference to the Combines Investigation Act, and I pause at this stage to say something about that act, because I think there is a tendency on the part of hon. members to misapprehend just what the possibilities are of investigating and remedying under the Combines Investigation Act. The purpose of that act is not to examine the reasonableness of prices; that is not the primary purpose of the Combines Investigation Act. It is to ascertain, inquire and investigate. The purpose of the act is to provide for investigation of trade combinations, trusts, mergers or monopolies which are alleged to have operated to the detriment of the public by restraining trade unduly. And in the administration of that act each case must be carefully and fully examined, not only with respect to a particular incident, but in many instances over a period of years.
The element of combination in itself greatly adds to the problem of investigation, because it is necessary to deal not only with the actions of a particular firm, but the relation of such actions to the practices followed by others alleged1 to be members of the combination. In practically all cases there must be careful examination of the business records of those alleged to be parties to the offence. This requires work by those who are trained to make such examinations over a considerable period, when a group of companies is involved.
It is not at all unusual for one hundred man-days or more to be spent on this phase of the investigation. This must be followed by careful analysis of the evidence so obtained, and then a period of hearings where those involved in the investigation are given an

Prices Committee
opportunity to offer further evidence and to reply to any allegations which may have been made against them. The right of those against whom any misconduct is alleged, to be given notice of such allegation, and reply thereto if they so desire, is carefully guarded in all investigations under the act. And the commissioner avoids anything in the nature of summary findings without giving those who may be affected adequate opportunity to make explanations or replies. This care to avoid any unfairness to those who may be involved in an investigation underlies the general practice not to make any disclosures as to firms which may be under investigation, except when a report is published.
Suspicion would be easily aroused if the other course were followed, that firms being investigated were guilty of misconduct, even though when the investigation was concluded there was no such finding.
As I have been asked to say something about what is 'being done under the Combines Investigation Act, I think I can tell the house that at the present time six major inquiries are being proceeded with, that the report in one case is expected before long and that t'he others should be made during the next few months.
During the past year the combines commissioner himself has been absent from Canada for altogether about six months attending various international conferences devoted to the preparation and discussion of a charter for an international trade organization. As a member of the Canadian delegation the commissioner attended the sessions in London, New York and Geneva, and has only recently returned from the conference at Havana. I may say that his services in connection with the preparation of that section of the charter dealing with international cartels have been most highly regarded by representatives of other countries, and I feel that he has made a substantial contribution to the development of the arrangements proposed to deal with the abuses of cartels.
His work in this field is directly related to the recommendations in the cartel report which was tabled in the House of Commons and which has been referred to 'by several members. His work in this field has not proceeded as rapidly as he would have liked. I have mentioned the six major inquiries which are now proceeding and1 which I understand involve more than fifty companies, large and small, in various fields. In addition, a number of other matters are subject to less intensive investigation or are under consideration.
So that hon. members may understand the administration of the Combines Investigation Act, and I think they should be interested, may I say that the activities are carried on by the commissioner with the assistance of a staff of only ten investigators. Of course counsel are engaged when required. This staff is not considered by the commissioner to be sufficient. The government has given the commissioner full support in any request he has made for an increase in staff but it is very difficult to get investigators who are qualified for this kind of work. It is not easy to secure persons who possess the full qualifications for investigation into the complex problems of trade restraints. Even when appointments are made it is necessary to undertake careful training before such persons are fully equipped to assist in investigations.
The combines investigation staff has also undertaken a preliminary study of the trend in amalgamations and mergers in Canada and is bringing together the available information on such developments. Attention is also being given to general questions affecting patents and trademarks in so far as they are related to amendments made to the act in 1946. I believe that the outline I have given indicates a full measure of activity on the part of the commissioner in relation to domestic combinations as well as international cartels.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
There are two deputy commissioners. Deputy Commissioner Whiteley is authorized to exercise the powers of Commissioner McGregor when he is out of Canada.
There is something I want to say about this Combines Investigation Act. A completely new phase of this act set in on August 31, 1946, with the passage of the amendments of that year. Since that date, which is something like twenty months ago, there have been three ways in which an inquiry may be initiated under the Combines Investigation Act. One is by formal application by six persons under section
Prices Committee

11.	There has not been one such formal application since August 31, 1946. We hear a lot from members of parliament and a little from the public, although not very much, about combines that are being formed, about monopolies, about imperfect competition, about quasi-monopolies and so on, but, as I say, from August 31, 1946, during this phase of the administration of the Combines Investigation Act, there has not been one formal application made for the investigation of a combine. That is point number one.
The second way in which an inquiry may be initiated is by the commissioner moving of his own motion, if he has reason to believe that a combine exists or is being formed. His activities are going on all the time and I have done something to describe them here.
The third way is on direction of the minister. For the nine years previous to 1946 there had to be either a direction by the minister or a formal application; the commissioner could not move of his own motion. I think there was some direction by the minister during that time. Now that the commissioner can proceed of his own motion there is very little occasion for the minister to give any direction. The minister does not have sent to him any evidence on which he can act. I have had just a handful of letters. They have suggested that a combine might exist in connection with certain things. I have handed such letters on at once to the commissioner with instructions that the matter be investigated. But that is a different thing from instituting formal inquiry.

My statement included
everything that I received, and I have received only a few letters.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: I wanted to know if the minister's statement applied to any information or complaints he has received from members of the house as well as from the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Absolutely. There is a
popular impression, and it may be true, that one of the major causes for the recent rise in prices in this county is the existence of monopolies, the existence of combines and the existence of imperfect competition. One of the duties, one of the responsibilities and one of the powers at any rate of this parliamentary committee will be to ascertain how far that is true. The committee is not being set up to go after persons who are alleged to be operating combines, but if the evidence before the committee shows that that is the case,

that evidence will be of assistance in the administration of the Combines Investigation Act.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: Will the minister permit a question before he leaves that particular phase?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
I am afraid you are spoiling my speech. I think the same observation would apply to what I have called the profiteering section of the wartime prices and trade regulations. I am not charged with the administration of those regulations, although the hon. member for Lake Centre appeared to think yesterday that I was, because he was calling upon me to give all sorts of facts and statements and rulings about the administration of that section.
I thoroughly understand why the wartime prices and trade board has not had many prosecutions under that section. There is nothing definite about the offence of charging prices which are greater than those which are just and reasonable. It is very hard to get something definite upon which to proceed. When there were ceilings and established prices those persons charging in excess of those prices could be prosecuted. I think some years ago there were successful prosecutions under that section and in certain cases you can get such prosecutions. This committee is not being set up as a prosecuting body. However, if the evidence before the committee discloses that prices have been charged which are clearly greater than those which are reasonable and proper, it would appear to me that the administration of that section of the wartime prices and trade regulations would be easier and more effective.
As the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) says, the parliamentary committee will let in the light and create public understanding and do away with misapprehensions and illusions as to the causes of the rise1 in prices. It will get the truth into the public mind and into the government's mind, into the mind of the House of Commons and into the mind of the opposition. We certainly do not pretend to be in possession of all the knowledge and all the wisdom, and I think nobody in the house is. But here is an opportunity for getting at the truth by investigation. That is one thing the committee can do.
Another thing is this. It perhaps may lead to legislative proposals by the government to meet certain situations. I do not know about that; I have nothing in mind. Thirdly it will assist in the ways I have mentioned, administratively, in what the government is now doing.

Prices Committee
Perhaps it will be of interest for me to say while on the Combines Investigation Act, that the policy of the government has been to support the administration of the act. I took occasion in speaking to a gathering in Quebec city last June to outline our policy in that regard, and with the indulgence of the house I will read two paragraphs of what I said on that occasion:
The success of the program of orderly decontrol depends upon healthy competition among business firms being at the same time restored. Some businessmen appear to have welcomed the absence of price competition during the period of extreme shortages under price control and to be reluctant to return to the system of a free market. It is important, however, that the expanding freedom permitted by decontrol be not used to make private restrictive arrangements which would deprive the public of the benefits produced by independent competitive enterprise.
The maintenance of a competitive economy in Canada as a matter of public policy was reaffirmed by parliament in amendments made to the Combines Investigation Act at the last session. This action was taken in recognition of the fact that as the emergency controls are removed, the public must look to active price competition rather than to any government control agency for its protection. I am, of course, not now referring to those segments of our economy such as public utilities and so forth, where government regulation or government ownership is substituted for competition as the regulating factor.
The very interesting speech made yesterday by the hon. member for Lake Centre did not make clear to me what his views were with regard to the Combines Investigation -Act. I do not think, upon reflection, that he expressed any. Certainly the tone and manner of his speech was one of accusation against the government, but I must say I never heard anyone speak so. accusingly and at the same time remain so uncommitted as the hon. member for Lake Centre did yesterday. I was interested because there is not a member of this house who has used more violent language over a period of years than he has about a subject very close to this. I have run through some of his speeches and I find that he has been complaining of the catechizing and interrogating of individuals by the government, the harrying and hounding of honest businessmen, interference with private lives, private property and private industry, snooping and having an army of snoopers-these are the things we have been attacked for during the last three years by the hon. member for Lake Centre.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: Is that the reason why you are not acting that way now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
We certainly are not. But yesterday the hon. member left himself in such a position that, he could say to one section of the public that he sailed into the government for not enforcing the Combines Investigation Act, and could say to another section of the public, a section which, I think, is far more influential with his party, that he did nothing but ask a few questions.
I do not propose to discuss price policy in any detail today because I anticipate there will be a better opportunity in the future, and it is not the question before us. The questions before us are the two I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks. I may say, in passing, that the policy of the government with regard to prices is, I think, the most reasonable policy to pursue having in mind the steadily accelerating impact of world events. There comes a time when a country can do only so much. Certainly proposals have been made with regard to the reduction of prices by the leader of the opposition and we have anticipated the budget debate by getting into a discussion of taxation. I understood the leader of the opposition the other night to say that he thought the time had come for indirect taxes to be removed. I do not think he would advocate the removal of all indirect taxes; that would be too much, and so the hon. member for Lake Centre tried to set the matter right yesterday by saying that the official opposition is mow in favour of the removal of the sales tax. I do not need to give my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) any advice as to how seriously concerned he should be over the advice he gets from the opposition. Some of it will be good, some of it will be bad, none of it will be disinterested, and very little of it will be given to help him. But the worst feature of it will be that it will vary from month to month and year to year.
Prior to the time the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Maedonnell) came into the house, the leading financial critic of the opposition was the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman). The hon. member for Rosedale made a speech when I was minister of finance and I remember it very clearly. He argued what? For the abolition of the sales tax? No; he argued for an increase in the sales tax. His remarks will be found at page 3299 of Hansard of July 9, 1946, and to the present Minister of Finance I suggest this may be their position next year. The hon. member for Rosedale said:
While there are some arguments against the extension of the sales tax, there are few when food, which bulks so largely ,in the average housewife's expenditure, is exempted as I recommend. Very few of our people today-know there is already a sales tax imposed at the wholesale level. Such a tax does not discourage *the worker from working, and there is fairness in. a tax policy based on the principle that the
Prices Committee

more one spends, the more one pays. There is nothing obligatory about paying a tax if one does not purchase; but unfortunately the great growth in instalment sales in normal times is a clear indication that most people will spend if they have the money and even when they have not. Let the worker have more take-home pay if we are to encourage production. Other indirect or non-incentive destroying taxes must be found if we are to keep our economy in high gear. I may be asked, how does it help in what *way we pay our taxes, when they have to come out of the same pocket anyway. The answer is that under the present system the pocket is only half full because the high individual tax rates discourage work, enterprise and production. Under a system such as I propose the same amount of taxes would have to be paid, but we would have fuller pocketbooks out of which to pay them.
I bring that to the attention of my colleague the Minister of Finance, to take into account along with the proposals that were made yesterday-in correction of the proposals that were made the day before.
I want to say something about the complaint I have against the C.C.F. The C.C.F. is talking about subsidies. The great policy of the C.C.F. is subsidies. They want to get the government back into a policy of subsidizing the articles that the people of the country buy. I think that if they will talk to some of their friends in the Labour party of Great Britain, to some of the more responsible ones, they will find that that government wishes it could get rid of subsidies. They feel they have got a tiger by the tail; they do not dare let go, and they hate to hang on. It is building up an elaborate system of subsidization- I am not talking about England; I should not be talking about England; I am talking about this country. I think it was extremely sound for this government to disentangle itself from that insidious subsidy system. It has got all kinds of things against it as a system in time of peace.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
What about the tariff system?
Mr. COLD WELL; That is a subsidy.
Mr. ILSLEY; Let me deal with these subsidies at the moment.
Mr. COLD WELL; You are trying to pick the one to suit your purpose.
Mr. ILSLEY; The complaint I wish to make is of a tendency on the part of the C.C.F. speakers to misuse a part of a speech which I made last year with regard to the value and use of subsidies. I shall quote from my hon. friend the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell). I have also the same complaint to make with regard to a speech made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum),

and I made it the other day. The leader of the C.C.F. opposition, said, as reported at page 763 of Hansard:
Hon. members will recall that last April the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) pointed out that the taxpayers and consumers of Canada had been saved enormous sums of money through subsidies. He computed those savings as in the neighbourhood of $2,500 million a year, on an expenditure of $200 million. In other words, for every dollar we spent we saved ourselves, either as taxpayers or consumers, twelve and a half dollars.
Now, I should like to point out the highly tentative and extremely guarded nature of the estimate.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
It was your statement.
Mr. ILSLEY; Well, I will read my statement. What I complain about is that the statement is cited and used as if I were making a weighty and carefully computed estimate. I remember so distinctly the occasion in the house. I was pressed by the hon. gentleman who sits behind the leader of the C.C.F. party. I was pressed repeatedly, "Make an estimate; make an estimate." I knew if I made an estimate-I knew no estimate was possible- it would be nothing more than a guess, and therefore I guarded it so I thought it would not be thrown back as what I said was saved to the country. This is what I said, as reported at page 1926 of the daily edition of Hansard of April 1, 1947:
The .following estimate gives some indication of the strain and difficulty which would have developed in the Canadian economy without price control. It is based on the assumption that in the absence of price control prices would have risen in recent years to the same extent that they rose in world war I and its aftermath. Nobody knows whether they would or would not, or would have risen higher.
Later I said:
If we assume, I say, that prices have risen, without control, just to the same extent proportionately, year by year, as they did in the period from 1914 to 1919, then these are the results you get: the consumers would have had to spend an average of nearly $8 billion between 1942 and 1946.
But it was a very theoretical assumption. Understand, I believe that the subsidy system during the war was an excellent system. I am glad we resorted to that system during the war; but under these conditions I think it is a bad peacetime system and I would hate to see this country get entangled into a subsidy system again. I would hate it for various reasons. I can give those reasons on a later occasion, but this is what I feel about that subsidy system.

Prices Committee

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: Will the minister not say that it is a good system in the face of the emergency which confronts us now?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: No, I would not regard it as a good system in the present emergency.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Over twenty-one points in a year.
Mr. ILSLEYr: Yes, but I do not know when you would ever get out, and what happens is that you keep your tax level up higher than it ought to be by reason of that growing snowball of subsidies, whereby all the citizens pay for the supplies to some of the citizens. It effects a certain type of redistribution of wealth which is far less scientific, far less equitable and far less just than the type of redistribution of wealth effected by the graduated income tax. And electorally it is dangerous; because when a great many of the consumer goods are subsidized by the state you inevitably get candidates vying with one another as to who will favour the higher subsidies, who will buy the largest share of the loaf of bread.
Coming back to the matter before the house, I shall conclude by saying I believe this inquiry, while it will be a very difficult one to conduct, can prove of great value for the reasons which I have mentioned. The feature of the proposal that gives me most concern is the extent of the field covered in the terms of reference. It is not going to be easy; it is not going to be an enviable task to select certain parts of the field for concentrated attention and effective investigation, but if we want to destroy the value of the committee, rob it of all prestige and make its task impossible, the surest way to do it is to give it still further studies, still greater powers, still larger responsibilities and more elaborate and detailed subjects for investigation.
The scope of this committee should be kept within practical limits, otherwise we shall lose the substance by grasping at the shadow. I hope that the house will, without too much additional debate, assent to the appointment of the committee and to the terms of reference which are contained in the notice of motion. Later some compelling urgency may require extension of the terms of reference, but to increase enormously the responsibilities of a committee, which, as now proposed, will be great, will bring the committee and its activities into disrepute.
There has been some suggestion that some parties in this house may boycott the committee and refuse to appoint members. That, of course, was what the Soviet union did at the last general assembly of the united nations
in respect of three very important matters, but I should hate to see this tactic adopted here. I hope also that no members of the committee will prejudge the issues, as the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) indicated the other night he had already done.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: Before the minister takes his seat may I ask him the question I sought to ask him earlier? I apologize for asking it at that time. A committee has to stick to its terms of reference. Will the minister say wherein the terms of reference show authority for the committee to examine monopolistic practises?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the resolution proposed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) reads:
That a select committee of this house be appointed to examine and to report from time to time as to (a)_ the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living; (b) prices which have been raised above levels justified by increased costs; (c) rises in prices due to the acquiring, accumulating or withholding from sale by any persons,
Prices Committee

firms or corporations of any goods beyond amounts reasonably required for the ordinary purposes of their businesses.
That the committee shall have power to appoint from among its members such subcommittees as may be deemed advisable or necessary to deal with specific phases of the enquiry, and power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee.
That the committee shall have leave to sit while the house is sitting;	,
That seven members of the committee shall constitute a quorum;
That the committee shall have power to engage the services of counsel, accountants and other necessary assistants who shall be paid out of the appropriation for parliament.
The resolution then names the members of the committee. There are sixteen, nine being members of the government, and of those nine there are one minister of the cabinet and four parliamentary assistants. There are four members of the Progressive Conservative party, two members of the C.C.F. and one member of the Social Credit party. The house will realize therefore, that the cabinet has complete control of the committee.
Immediately after the introduction of the motion by the Prime Minister, on February 2, an amendment was proposed by the leader of this party asking that the committee be empowered to make recommendations and that it be given certain other powers. A subamendment wa3 moved by the C.C.F. The debate continued that afternoon and evening and the following afternoon and into the evening, and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) rose and argued against the amendments being in order. He was supported in his arguments by the Prime Minister, and in due course the Speaker ruled the amendments out of order.
That to me seems strange because on the previous evening I had heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) discussing constitutional questions, and in his argument he contended that this amendment would be restricting the work of the committee. There was certainly a difference of opinion on the other side.
When we read the remarks of the Prime Minister at the time he was leader of the opposition in 1934, at which time Mr. Bennett was prime minister, on the occasion of the introduction of the proposal for the price spreads committee, and when we listen now to the right hon. gentleman's observations in proposing this resolution, and, later, his objection to having the scope of the present committee enlarged, as was proposed, to enable

the committee to do the work expected of it, it is most difficult to understand his line of reasoning at his time.
One hon. member has asked him to answer certain questions when he replies; and I should like him to say, if this committee is set up, whether we shall have an opportunity of discussing on the floor of the house dur-: ing this session reports of the committee as and when submitted.
As has been pointed out, we have the Combines Investigation Act, which provides all the machinery necessary for the fullest possible kind, of inquiry into any matter preventing or lessening production, or any matter respecting trade; and clause (c) of the first paragraph of the resolution before us seems to have given rise to some doubt, as between the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), and some other members, as to whether that would be restricting clause (c) in the resolution as it stands.
We have ample legislation under the wartime prices and trade board regulations to prosecute for profiteering and the like. The people of Canada today want action and not a delaying method' as is proposed in the setting up of this futile committee. We have in Canada the eight per cent sales tax, collected, with few exceptions, on processed commodities of all kinds. As one of my party points out, this tax applies to bacon and other processed agricultural commodities which are quite essential. We have in these hidden taxes a pyramiding incubus on every member of the consuming public in the dominion today.
Federal taxes, direct and indirect, amounted per capita to $22.41 in 1913, and in 1939 the per capita had risen to $38.67. In 1947, the year just past, that per capita tax was $192.97. The tax has multiplied over five times since the beginning of the second world war; and it has greatly added to the cost of production and the cost of living in Canada, a fact which government officials have ignored in compiling the cost of living index and of production for this nation.
Up to the present time in this debate we have heard from five ministers of the crown. I have referred to the minister of external affairs. As the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) so well pointed' out yesterday, the minister spoke rather from the point of view of a private citizen than as one assuming his responsibility as a member of the cabinet. He professed that he did not know how this situation had been brought about or how we could come out of this chaos.

Prices Committee
Then the Minister	of Labour	(Mr. Mitchell), in his usual breezy fashion, gave us a lecture; and this afternoon we have just heard the	Minister	of	Justice,	who
throughout most of the war years was Minister of Finance and was responsible for the cost of living legislation during that period. I have always admired the Minister of Justice for his conscientious and serious attitude *toward the problems of the day, but as I followed him this afternoon I could not tell whether he personally favoured this resolution. I have worked in committees with the minister before, when he was doing things he would rather not have had a hand in, because it was the will of the government. What I wish to refer to more particularly, however, is the speech delivered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), which in my opinion, was inaccurate and certainly misleading. It reminded me of a chap who in distress with his particular office, was whistling in the dark for the time being.
The Minister of Agriculture said that the farmer was now receiving more for agricultural products than at any other time in the history of the country. I said, during his i emarks, that was not a statement of fact, and I still believe it to be untrue. He then took the year 1918, immediately on the close of the first world war, and the year 1947, two years after the end of the second world war, and he based a comparison on these two periods. Then may I remind this house that, according to government statistics, in a pamphlet put out by themselves, in the war period 1914-18 the farmers received 29 per cent of the national income, whereas in the recent war, 1939-45, the farmers received 18 per cent of the national income. All those figures and percentages are from government statistics.
Then, during that speech he referred to January, and he says that at the present time -that is, January, 1918-wheat is $2 for the latter part of the year and $1.55 for the first part of the year. I wish to say that under existing federal legislation on wheat the farmer-producer is paid only SI .35, basis Fort William, which means an average of $1.17 initial payment at the elevator and participation certificates. True enough, the minister announced at Brockville that legislation would be brought in to make the basic payment $1.55, basis Fort William, which would be approximately $1.37 at the elevator. So even that statement was misleading.
Then the right hon. gentleman, in answer to a question about the cost of farm implements said, as reported in Hansard at page 805:
When one starts to talk about the cost of production, everything must be considered. And everything is taken into consideration, the cost of production in Canada is 77-7 per cent of what it is in the United States.
If that be true, it is strange that farm implements of Canadian manufacture have been selling at a much higher figure than have farm implements of United States manufacture. While I have no quotation for the present day, I want to refer to some figures as of the spring of 1947 and to put them on record.
As of March 1, 1947, to purchase a Farmall M. tractor, International company tractor, in Canada required 1,225 bushels of wheat; in the United States, 710 bushels of wheat. To purchase a 3-furrow International tractor plow in Canada required 151 bushels of Wheat; in the United States, 82 bushels. To purchase a 24-run International double disc seeder in Canada required 270 bushels of wheat; in the United States, 146 bushels. To purchase a 10-foot International binder in Canada required 333 bushels of wheat; in the United States, 184 bushels. To purchase the same tractor in Canada would require slightly over the price of eleven finished 1,000-pound steers that I have spoken of, while in the United States the same type of tractor would require the proceeds of only slightly over six such animals. In the matter of hogs it would require forty-six select hogs weighing 210 pounds in Canada or twenty-six such hogs in the United States to purchase the same type of tractor. After all, what you can purchase with the goods that the farmer produces is what he is interested in.
Then I have a report of the remarks made by the right hon. gentleman at Brockville to t'he Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and he made reference to that- meeting in his

Prices Committee

speech the other day. He told those people that price ceilings on meat would be announced in the near future, to cover the price of meat in accordance with the price of beef announced under the United Kingdom contract of January 2. Then he made a peculiar statement with respect to butter, as reported in the paper. It is hard to follow, when compared with his remarks in this house the other day on this resolution. As reported here, he told those people that he thought they would be better off if this ceiling had been only fifty-five cents on butter rather than seventy and some cents. It is hard to reconcile those two statements and to follow his reasoning. He says:
I personally feel that the floor price of fifty-five cents per pound on this commodity would have been much better as it would have then sold at approximately fifty-eight cents per pound to the customer and farmers would be receiving as much as they are now getting for this item . . .
