maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Yes. I am not going to say anything about the feathers, but I am going to say this. It will take even the political ingenuity and wiles of the Prime Minister to keep these two warring chickens at peace under his wing much longer. He will have to make up his mind sooner or later which of these chickens really belongs to him, because I think one or the other of them will have to be disowned shortly as a duckling.
I do not know why it should have required so much elaboration on the part of some hon. members who participated in this debate to demonstrate that there is a rising cost of living. Surely we do not need to take up the time of the House or Commons to demonstrate a fact that everyone of us must be confronted with in his own life, in his own riding, in his every contact, namely, that we are faced right now with a rise in the cost of living which has reached alarming proportions. It is bearing very heavily on people of small means, and more especially, I think, on people on small fixed incomes than on anybody else, because there are a great many people in this country whose incomes have not increased perceptibly, certainly far from being in fair proportion to this vaulting cost of living.
In the debate yesterday mention was made of the fact that in the month of December the cost of living increased 2-3 points. But that is not the whole story. There are two other features in the report issued yesterday by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics which are equally worthy of note. The first is that the increase in the cost of living in 1947 was 21-3 points. The other factor worthy of note is that, while the general cost of living increased 2-3 points in the month of December, the factor of food costs increased three and a half points, and it has now reached the figure of 182-2. I should like to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the reason for that last shocking increase in the cost of food is attributable to government policy, to what the business community has come to regard as the equivalent of sabotage, and I refer to "Abbotage". What I mean by that is precisely this: the responsibility for that increase in the cost of living rests squarely on the shoulders of this government, because this increase in the cost of food in the past two months is directly attributable to the policies announced by this government late in November and put into force without any reference whatsoever to parliament.
That is factor No. 1, the existence of this soaring increase in the cost of living. The second is the relationship of that increase to government policy. We cannot dissociate the two. It simply cannot be done. To ask this committee to go to work and to investigate the cost of living, and to say to it at the same time, you may not consider questions of government policy, or the extent to which government policy is responsible for reduced production in Canada, particularly of foodstuffs, or for high prices, is to make a mockery and a sham of the appointment of the committee at all; that is what the government have done deliberately. If they had meant this committee to be really effective, to accomplish something, they would not have trimmed its wings before it was even appointed; they would have welcomed the amendment put forward from this side of the house. If there was any hope at all of bringing any constructive and effective end to the labours of this committee it rested solely on the addition of the amendment moved by my leader. The government have succeeded in taking objection to that on the ground of order, and it has gone by the boards. This poor committee is left now with a very narrow field in which it cannot hope to do anything effective.
The blunders of the government in its control policy, and the equal blunders of the government in its decontrol policy, along with the facts I have mentioned, are responsible for the mess which exists today, a deliberate government creation.
In his remarks on Monday, the Prime Minister was very careful to exclude entirely any attempt to deal with the causes of the rise in the cost of living. He said that he was not going to deal with them at that time. Why not? The house is entitled to know from the lips of the leader of the government just why, in his opinion, the cost of living is reaching its present shocking proportions. But no; that was a subject taboo as far as the Prime Minister was concerned, and, I think, for obvious reasons.
The third factor in the situation I should like to refer to is this. The people of this country are aroused to the fact that the cost of living is running away from them and they are looking in the direction of Ottawa at the present time for some action to halt it. Why? This is the same government that told them all during the war what a wonderful job they were doing in holding
Prices Committee

down the cost of living. They did not make so much noise of the fact that they were holding ceilings on wages and on salaries at the same time; but they used the funds of the countiy to broadcast the boast that they were doing such a wonderful job in holding down the cost of living. Is it any wonder today that the Canadian people, faced with the most rapid increase in the cost of living ever recorded in Canadian history, are looking to the same government and saying, "Why, you bragged about holding down the cost of living before? Here is the runaway cost of living today. You are the people responsible. What are you going to do about it now?" Yes, Mr. Speaker, the chickens are coming home to roost. Right -now the sky over Ottawa is black with the chickens coming home to roost on this government.
I said something about the hopelessness of the task of the committee, trimmed as it now is by the deliberate intent of the government. The committee is, of course, not to be permitted to make a single recommendation. Sixteen members of the house, who are expected to have some sense of responsibility, are being asked to serve on the committee, and the government is saying to them, "Well, gentlemen, we will permit you to make an inquiry into the situation. We will not let you go very far; we will confine you within a very narrow groove; you can make a report on what you find out; you can report certain facts-if you can come to an agreement on what the facts are-but don't you dare say *what you think ought to be done to meet the situation disclosed by the facts. We don't trust you to do that." Oh, no; only the government is permitted apparently to deal with questions of that kind, because the government is hiding behind the silly assertion that that must be government policy. Well, if they have a policy, and this is within the realm of government policy, then why on earth does the government not -bring some policy before us? We have not had any policy brought before us by the government in this debate. The field is a vacuum at the present time. It is about time somebody got into it. The government will not open its mouth on the subject of its own policy; and now it says it will not permit a committee of the house, a responsible committee presumably, to open their mouths on the subject of what ought to be done to meet a situation which is rapidly reaching critical proportions.
Here is the test of the good faith of the government in this matter. If the government really means this committee to be effective; if the government really intends that light 
shall be shed in dark places, then the course open to the government is perfectly clear, the course it ought to follow, and that is to say to that committee: "No holds barred, no clipping of your wings. Go in there and get to the bottom of the whole situation"-the sort of thing the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) would like to see done by a parliamentary committee if he were spokesman for the government and not simply the mouthpiece of his own views and those of the C.C.F.
By what was done, in the objection to the amendment of my leader, the government has not simply emasculated the committee, as was suggested by one hon. member yesterday. It has gone the whole way and completely eviscerated the committee. Why should questions of policy be excluded? I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that what is needed right now is a courageous approach to the question of the cost of living, and it must be made a matter of policy, and made so immediately.
Let us have some policy. There is no government policy at the present time. The government is acting like a dog in the manger. It has no policy of its own and it will not allow anyone to devise or declare a policy. The Prime Minister closes his lips on the subject; and yet the government says to the committee, "You shall not occupy the field of government policy. That must remain a vacuum," even though the government boasts a majority of members on the committee. It has nine members to seven, and a member of the cabinet and four parliamentary assistants are among the nine.
I wondered at the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in this house the day before yesterday. He made a great parade of what he considered to be the accomplishments of the government in the field of food production and in ministering to the lot of the farmers; and yet he and the administration of which he is a member were not prepared to let this committee review that subject. Oh, no. It will be left to the Minister of Agriculture and the ministers in the house to make a great parade of what the government thinks it has accomplished. The government will not allow a committee to review such questions. They say, "Oh, no. We are quite confident in our policy and the success of what we have done." But when you suggest that the question of policy should be referred to a committee on which the government has a majority of members, the answer is, "No. We cannot risk this tender plant in the hands of any committee of the house." This shibboleth of government policy has now become a sacred cow and it is inviolable.

Prices Committee
The Minister of Justice this afternoon took great pains to suggest that somehow or other there are powers available to the committee that are not available to the government today. He laboured long but he did not convince even himself. What about the Combines Investigation Act? I do not need to go over the story again. It has been told time and again in this debate, but never more clearly or more eloquently than by my leader on Monday or by the hon. member for Lake Centre yesterday afternoon.
Everything in the way of power that the committee has, or will have, is possessed today by the government and by government boards. Everything in the way of power which the committee will have, the government and its boards have had all along. The combines investigation branch have had these powers for years. The wartime prices and trade board, with a substantial enforcement branch, has had all the powers for the last half dozen years. And what is the sorry record that the Minister of Justice has to come into this house this afternoon and confess to? It was a pretty sad tale we heard from him. No wonder he looked so sad this afternoon as he made his confession.
Here is the record of the government, presided over by the Prime Minister who claims the parentage of the Combines Investigation Act, and who said in this house on Monday that it was the policy of the government to give vigilant enforcement to the act. What is the record? Six major investigations are being proceeded with at the present time. If the minor investigations amounted to anything the Minister of Justice would have told us about them, but he did not mention them. There are these six major inquiries being proceeded with at the present time and, believe it or not, the government expects to have one finished soon. Others may be started, but where will they start and when? What have they done with information, the kind of information the Minister of Justice has been passing on to them, the kind of information which the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) said he had done his duty in passing on to the Minister of Justice, and which the Minister of Justice apparently has passed on to the combines investigation branch?
Let us take what comfort we can from the fact that one investigation is likely to be completed shortly. By way of extenuation of this sorry tale, the Minister of Justice gets up and says in effect, "Well, it is not much of a showing, I admit; but, after all, the combines 5849-58
investigation commissioner was out of the country most of the year". It is to be hoped that the commissioner will not have to be sent away very often or very soon, because this government apparently will be helpless without him.
I recall to you, Mr. Speaker, that in 1946 the government asked for power to appoint assistant commissioners, deputy commissioners who were to be clothed with the same powers as theretofore had been enjoyed by the commissioner himself, and the house gladly acceded to the proposal. You will find it embodied in chapter 44 of the statutes of 1946. Power is given there in the most express terms to the government to appoint one or more persons as deputy commissioners, and they are to have the powers and duties of the commissioner whenever he is absent or unable to act. It is provided in section 3:
The commissioner may authorize a deputy commissioner to make inquiry regarding any. matter into which the commissioner has power to inquire, and when so authorized a deputy commissioner shall perform such of the duties of the commissioner and may exercise such of the powers of the commissioner as such deputy commissioner is, by this act or any regulations made thereunder, required or authorized to perform or exercise.
Is it not a pity that we have to sit in this house and listen to the Minister of Justice making such a feeble excuse for the fact that he has so sorry a record to report in the enforcement of the Combines Investigation Act?
The other source of power which the government has enjoyed for the last half dozen years is contained in the general order in council which establishes the wartime prices and trade board, P.C. 8528, with a number of amendments, under the sections dealing with offences, penalties and prosecutions. These sections have been there all these years.
The Minister of Justice this afternoon called these the profiteering sections. Apparently they are, and they will be profiteering sections until the government puts iron into its soul and gets busy and enforces these sections and makes them anti-profiteering sections. The Minister of Justice did not deny that they have the power. As a matter of fact, it would be difficult to conceive of language broader than the language to be found in section 8 of the general order. I do not wish to dwell on this because the subject was referred to earlier in the debate. But let me give one or two short quotations. Section 8 (1) reads:
No person shall sell or offer for sale or supply any goods or services at a price that is higher than is reasonable and just . . .
Prices Committee

And again:
(3) No person shall
(a) acquire, accumulate or withhold from sale any goods beyond an amount which is reasonably required . . .
And so on. You will find that followed, Mr. Speaker, by a number of other similar provisions buttressing the general powers of the board and leading on to section 9 which provides as follows:
Any person who contravenes or fails to observe any regulation or order shall be guilty of an offence and liable upon summary conviction under part XV of the criminal code or, if the Attorney General of Canada-
And that is the Minister of Justice, let me remind you.
-or of any province so directs, upon indictment, to a penalty not exceeding five thousand dollars or to imprisonment for any term not exceeding two years or to both such fine and such imprisonment; . . .
The courts have the same penal power with respect to any director or officer of any company or corporation who is guilty of a similar offence.
Now the Minister of Justice has the temerity to come before the house this afternoon and say, "The reason we have had so few convictions under these sections is that the terms are so vague and indefinite." Can you devise any terms which are more clear and definite than those, Mr. Speaker? They would certainly be clear and definite enough in the hands of an administration that really meant business in the enforcement of this order; and if they are not clear and definite, whose responsibility is it but that of the Minister of Justice and the government of which he is still a member? If these terms were not clear and definite enough to enable the government successfully to prosecute those who were breaking the spirit and the letter of the law, then why did the government not, long since, amend this order in council? It was not for lack of power. It must have been for lack of will.
I take it that everybody in this house is in favour of the prosecution of profiteers. They certainly should be prosecuted. But I cannot see much evidence of a determination on the part of the present administration to use the powers it now has to prosecute those who may be profiteering at the public expense.
Let me now deal for a moment with the straw man which the Minister of Justice set up this afternoon in trying to leave with us the impression that somehow this proposed committee would have powers which are not enjoyed by the wartime prices and trade board or the combines investigation branch. Where does he find those broader powers? They do

not exist in the resolution. What is this committee authorized to do? It may inquire into and make findings of fact on:
(a)	the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living;
(b)	prices which have been raised above levels justified by increased costs.
(e)	rises in prices due to the acquiring, accumulating or withholding from sale by any persons, firms or corporations of any goods beyond amounts reasonably required for the ordinary purposes of their businesses.
The committee will certainly have no more power than has the wartime prices and trade board or the combines investigation branch to inquire and make findings of fact or reports.
In the second place, the committee will not have the facilities or the personnel to do the work of inquiry as well as it could be done today by the combines investigation branch or the wartime prices and trade board. We heard the Minister of Justice this afternoon say that difficulty was experienced in getting investigators who were competent to do the work of investigation under the Combines Investigation Act. If it is so difficult to get investigators for that purpose, how is it to be expected that this committee will find it any easier to get the kind of investigators that are needed? Here are people who are making it a lifetime task, applying to it the training extending over years to qualify them to do the work of investigation. Yet the government says, "So far as doing anything in the present situation is concerned, we will close up shop as far as the combines investigation branch and the wartime prices and trade board are concerned: they have trouble in getting investigators". But somehow or another this committee is expected to find it possible to do the work of investigation that these other permanent bodies, with their qualified staff, somehow are not able to do. The whole thing just makes utter nonsense.
In the third place, I contend that the committee will not be able to work as fast and as expeditiously as either the wartime prices and trade board or the combines investigation branch can. When the government has any information, whether it be from the hon. member from New Westminster, the hon. member for Spadina or anybody else with regard to cases where profiteering is going on, all that either of those bodies has to do today is to say to a member of the investigation branch, "Get on your horse and go right into that business; take their books in hand and make a report". Compare that with the inevitable procedure in the committee. The committee has to meet. It has to set up its organization. Where is it to start? When is

Prices Committee
it to get around to the task of making the appointment of investigators, andi finding these people whom the Minister of Justice is finding it so difficult to get to do the work of investigation in the combines investigation branch, and then, start those people to work? We do not know how soon they will be able to start; andi when on earth, Mr. Speaker, do you think they will bring in a report? These investigators are going to take some time. These are not people whose task it is to be busy at investigation work all the time. And when do you think you will get the report discussing the findings of fact that the resolution now contemplates? The committee cannot possibly do as effective or as expeditious work as can be done today by the wartime prices and trade board or the combines investigation branch, if either or both of those bodies are set to work by the government to do the task that the people of Canada expect them to do.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, motions
drawn by the hand of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) must naturally invite scrutiny, and a little study of the actual text of this resolution is, I think, warranted.
The first of the three items assigned to the committee for examination and report is:
(a) the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) was at some pains the other evening to explain how this curious word "recent" found its way into the motion. He explained, for instance, that the committee had to have some starting point, and that, therefore, the word "recent" was inserted.
What does the word "recent" mean? We are dealing with the rise in the cost of living which did not begin within the last month, because figures I cited this afternoon show that for the past twelve months the cost of living has risen more than 21 points.
What does the word "recent" mean as applied to these facts? It is the kind of word which, I have no doubt, will invite discussion. But taking it on the basis offered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, we find he says that it will provide a starting point. I say it will also provide a stopping point; because, if the committee is confined in its inquiry into the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living, what will happen to the rise 5849-58J
which is going to continue from this point on, as the government sits back in its blundering, inefficient way, because the cost of living will continue to rise, in the face of the government's inaction. And anything in the way of further increase after the date of the passing of this motion-if it passes-does not fall within the scope of the inquiry of the committee.
The government has been wrong so often in its prognostications about increases in the cost of living that perhaps it is not necessary to remind the house that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) returned from England last October he undertook to unburden himself of the prophecy that the cost of living index would go up another couple of points, and that it might settle somewhere between 140 and 145. Think of that! That was only three months ago-and already the cost of living has reached 14S-3. So we know just about how much to expect from this government in the way of accurate prognostications as to movement in the cost of living. But these further increases are outside the scope of the inquiry.
Then, let us look at the language in paragraph (c) which says:
Rises in prices due to the acquiring, accumulating or withholding from sale by any persons, firms or corporations of any goods beyond amounts reasonably required for the ordinary purposes of their businesses.
I -was curious to find where that language came from; and it was with considerable interest I discovered that this clause is taken word for word from section 8 (3) (a) of the order establishing the wartime prices and trade board, the "profiteering" section. It is the same, word for word.
What does that mean? It means this, that there you have a provision which is the law of the land. The Prime Minister comes to the House of Commons and says, "appoint a select committee of the house to examine and report as to whether the law has been carried out," when the enforcement of the law is in the hands of the government, and is the government's responsibility.
Look at those three provisions. Every one of them is within the scope of the wartime prices and trade board order. Everyone of them has its full counterpart in the anti-profiteering section of the order. And, Mr. Speaker, what the government asks us to do is to inquire into the question whether or not the law has been observed. That is a fine example of respect for law and order! What can you expect from others, when the government itself does not know whether the law has been enforced by itself and its officers.
Prices Committee

One further comment with respect to the language of the resolution. It will be noted that paragraph (b) in the resolution refers to:
Prices which have been raised above levels justified by increased costs.
There was a curious commentary on the last word "costs" by the Secretary of State for External Affairs the other evening when, as reported at page 776 of Hansard, he said:
There may be a million things which are cost factors.
I can see that the committee has quite a task before it.
How is this committee to go about its work? I think that is worthy of consideration by the house. Well, first of all, the committee will have to be organized, and we expect a sonorous speech from the learned and honourable chairman of the committee, dripping with professions as to the noble purposes of the committee. That, of course, will take some time. It will be full of adulation of the Prime Minister. And may I interject here that if the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) does not succeed to the Liberal leadership it will not be for lack of adulation of the Prime Minister.
Then there will be the question of choosing counsel. There will be the further question of choosing investigators. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) says it is hard to get investigators. I do not know where on earth he will get all the investigators needed. There are in this country, I believe, something like
18,000	businesses which make returns to the government. I suppose it will take quite a few investigators to cover that field. Where are they to start? Are they to start with John Jones, or are they going to the Winnipeg grain exchange, or are they going to look into the livestock markets somewhere, or into the cabbage market? Where are they to start? There has not been the slightest indication, and I doubt if the chairman-designate of the committee knows, himself.
We are told it is not a fishing expedition. But where on earth are they to start? One expects that if there is any reason at all they will start with the complaints which have already been placed in the lap of the wartime prices and trade board. But then, that naturally invites the question. Well, if there is any basis at all for these complaints, why have they not been sifted through and action taken on them, if action is warranted?
So I do not know where the committee is going to go. However, we are told it is to be a fact-finding committee. That naturally raises the question:	Are they to find on the

facts of individual cases, or seek to make a general finding? Are they to look into the price of fresh vegetables and say, after due investigation, that John Jones bought cabbage at five cents a pound and sold it at eight cents a pound with a profit of three cents a pound and that, while the committee has diverging views on the facts, the majority think that two cents a pound would have been ample, and that three cents was too much? Are we to have about 10,000 or 20,000 cases of that kind; or is the committee to be invited to say that the increase in the cost of living has been due in some part to profiteering? How do they draw inferences of that kind? They cannot draw inferences of that kind without having made an investigation of a great many cases, because it would be most unfair to draw sweeping conclusions of that kind after reviewing only a few cases. So that I can imagine there is a tidy job of work to be done.
If they sit until doomsday they will not complete the whole task. And in the meantime the evidence is growing staler and staler every day. We shall have gone through two or three booms and a depression or two before the committee can possibly finish or possibly review all the business that is involved in the increase in the cost of living.
There is another point with which I should like to deal. Where complaints have been made to the present enforcement bodies and where the enforcement officers have actually reached the point where they are ready to take action, what will happen? Is prosecution to be delayed in order that this committee may further review the evidence? If these matters once get into court and the committee wants to review cases of that kind it will be told that they are sub judice and their hands will be tied.
What will this accomplish? A tide of public opinion has been raised over the rising cost of living because the public have heard the government's professions and have seen how they have not been kept. Instead of trying to meet the trainload of protests by the public, the Prime Minister is trying to turn the switch and send the train up a side spur so that it can never get back on the main track. He is hoping to see these protests stalled somewhere on the spur track far off the main line.
Undoubtedly he hopes to get some benefit from delay. He is hoping that something will turn up. Therefore he is practising 'his characteristic Fabian tactics of just sitting back and hoping that something will turn up.
He talks about the government wanting action. In the face of this resolution, can one

Prices Committee
imagine any greater casuistry than is contained in his words when he talks about action, when he asks the house to appoint a committee?
What is to come out of the findings of this committee? No one knows. Will they ever be debated in the house? Nobody knows. If the Prime Minister wants that action I submit that he is running away from action right now. Action should come from the government. This is simply a scheme to avoid facing the responsibility which belongs to the government. Obviously it hopes that the public will be fooled into thinking that the government is doing something when, in fact, its actions constitute nothing more than pretence and sham.
Parliament will be stifled by this resolution. You may be sure, Mr. Speaker, that when the occasion arises in the house objection will be taken to discussion of the cost of living, just as abjection was taken in 1946 when attempts were made to ask questions with regard to matters before the war expenditures and economies committee, and in 1947 in connection with matters before the public accounts committee. The whole resolution is simply a scheme on the part of the government to shirk its responsibilities.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first time since I came to parliament in 1940 that I recall the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and four of the senior members of the cabinet participating in a debate. I think it is equally significant that very few private members on the government side have had anything to say. I must conclude from the comments of the ministers that they are completely out of touch with public opinion in Canada today. We understand that cabinet ministers are busy men and that they carried great responsibilities during the war, but I think they should get out on the back concessions from time to time and talk to our farmers and fishermen and industrial workers to find out what the rise in the cost of living is doing to the people of Canada.
On many occasions during the war, both in parliament and throughout the country, I went out of my way to pay tribute to Canada's wartime Minister of Finance, who is now Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley). I do not think the minister did himself credit today with the speech he made in the debate. He dismissed quite lightly a carefully considered statement which was given previously in parliament when he estimated that the cost of subsidies to the wartime prices and trade board would be around $200 million a year
but that they saved the Canadian people over $2,500 million a year. I do not think the Minister of Finance pulled those figures out of the air. He had his advisers from the wartime prices and trade board before him. If he feels that he should state publicly now that he gave the people of Canada wrong advice, why does he not do so? I do not think it is becoming to a Minister of Justice to treat a carefully given statement as he did today.
He said today that those estimates were based on the assumption that we would have the same developments in Canada after world war II that we had after world war I. Perhaps he was wrong; perhaps we would have had an even more drastic increase in the cost of living had it not been for controls.
Then the minister had something to say about subsidies. During the supper recess I looked up Hansard and I found some comments which the minister made when he was justifying the payment of subsidies. As reported on pages 1882 and 1883 of Hansard of April 23, 1942, the minister dealt with this controversial problem. The government had been criticized because of the cost of the subsidies and he dismissed that criticism by saying that the proposed cost was not very much. He answered the criticism that the wartime prices and trade board could not estimate the cost of subsidies for a given period by saying that criticism was invalid. He answered the charge that dealers and producers were making fortunes out of the subsidies and he also answered the criticism that the subsidies were inflationary.
The minister gave the house a long list of items on which subsidies were paid, such as milk, footwear, leather garments and so on, as well as commodities which were being imported into Canada, such as cocoa, dried and evaporated fruits and so on down the line. Quite correctly the minister reminded the house that it was in the public interest that those commodities should be imported or supplied to our people and that price ceilings should be maintained. In concluding his remarks the minister enlisted the cooperation of the Canadian people by saying:
This policy is a test of the capacity of this democracy to organize and discipline itself in such a way as to wage total war on the economic front. I had many misgivings at the outset as to whether we could succeed. I now believe that we can: and will. We can only do so, however, if this parliament approaches its task of criticism in the proper spirit.
I should like to say a word about the remarks of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). I think those of us who listened to him felt that he made a most valuable con-
. Prices Committee

tribution to this debate. I am sure it takes a good deal of courage to be the only voice on the government side speaking out as he did. I hope that before the debate is over we shall hear from the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) and the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair), who have on previous occasions expressed their views when they were in conflict with the administration. I thank the hon. member for Spadina for the free advice which he gave to the members of this party. We accept his wisdom in the spirit in which it is given. I should like to ask him, if he were sitting over with us and if he knew that the people of Canada did not need a committee to tell them the cause of the recent rise in the cost of living, to tell them that prices have been raised to levels beyond their pocketbooks, what he would say.
Following the views expressed by -the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), I wish to say that I do not think there is any doubt that this committee will not have -an opportunity to report to parliament and have its report discussed. Hon. members on this side have been frustrated in every move they have made to get some teeth put into the resolution so that the committee may make recommendations. I should like to draw to the attention of the hon. member for Spadina and all hon. members citation 560 in Beauchesne's, third edition, which reads:
When the report does not contain any resolutions, recommendations or other propositions for consideration of the house, it does not appear that any further proceedings in reference to it as a report are necessary. Every session, select committees make reports of this description, containing a statement of facts, or of the evidence on the subject of inquiry; but as they do not contain any proposition which can be agreed to by the house, they are simply printed for the information of the members. I
I ask the hon. member for Spadina, does he think this parliament would be performing any useful public service if at this stage we set up a committee to investigate in accordance with the terms of reference and bring in a report a year from now? While cabinet ministers and all members of parliament are besieged with protests from the people of this country about the rising costs of living, it is proposed to set up a committee, and in the meantime nothing can be done. The experience we have had with committees and commissions is not reassuring to those who still have the hope that a committee of this sort might accomplish something.	.
The leader of this party yesterday made reference to the select committee on price spreads appointed in 1934 and reminded the

house that parliament passed a resolution setting up a committee on February 2, 1934. The committee quickly got to work, had its first meeting on February 22 and its last on June 22, then reported that its work had not been completed and recommended that it be continued by a royal commission. The royal commission had its first meeting on October 30, 1934, and its last on February 1, 1935. Its report was brought in on April 9, 1935. During that long period 270 witnesses were called and 440 exhibits were put in, and now one has to wade through 8,277 pages to find the kernels that are available among what is, in my opinion, a great deal of chaff. I submit that the people of Canada do not want any 8,277 page report at this stage.
An hon. MEMBER; Will you settle for less?

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Someone suggests it may be done in less. I submit that the situation is much more critical today than the situation which confronted Canada then.
Let me refer to two other investigating bodies that were set up. In 1937 a committee of the house was appointed to investigate the price of farm implements. That committee made recommendations and pointed out that the companies engaged in this business had over a period of years made substantial profits on the capital invested in each company. There were thirty-six recommendations in all.
In 1939 another investigation was made in Saskatchewan under a Liberal government. This Saskatchewan committee felt that nothing very much had resulted from the investigation in Ottawa, and it made some very useful recommendations. But I would remind the house that farm implements are still selling at prices away out of line with prices the farmers receive for their products. A twelve-foot combine in 1946 sold at Sturgis, Saskatchewan, where I live, for $3,421.35. The factory price was $2,308.25, a difference of $1,113.10; and if you deduct freight, the difference was $988.10. So that the government certainly does not require any further information on the farm implement situation.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) had a sessional paper brought down yesterday showing the special and accelerated depreciation allowances granted to the Massey-Harris Company and Cockshutt Plow, covering -each of the years 1939, 1940, and so on. This return shows that the Massey-Harris Company had- special depreciation over that period- amounting to $1,367,525.35 and Cockshutt Plow $1,936,943.99. So I submit, Mr. Speaker, that there is no need in February, 1948, for the parliament of Canada to set up any more committees to

Prices Committee
find out why farm implements are selling so high and why the people of Canada are complaining about the cost of living.
I looked over a speech which the Prime Minister delivered to the Canadian people on October 18, 1941, and I would remind the house that the situation which confronted us then was not, in my opinion, as serious as the situation today. There was no suggestion then that a parliamentary committee should be set up to investigate. The cost of living from the beginning of the war until October 1, 1941, had increased by only 14-6 points, whereas in the last twelve months the cost of living has increased by 21 points. On the first of January last the index stood at 148-3, and I venture to say at the present time the cost of living is up 50 points from the beginning of the war.
Listen to what the Prime Minister said in inviting the Canadian people to play ball with his administration on October 18, 1941:
We have heard much in recent weeks about rising prices. They have affected the budget of every family in Canada. We have heard and seen something of the dangers of inflation. But comparatively few of us, I imagine, understand those dangers fully, and what their effect may be upon our lives and our labours. By inflation we mean a rise in prices and costs brought about by abnormal conditions whereby our money is able to buy less of the things we need.
Rising prices unless controlled will make it more costly and therefore more difficult to finance the war. Rising prices, unchecked, will spread confusion and uncertainty in industry and trade. They will hinder production luul the proper distribution of supplies. They will make the cost of living rise more rapidly than wages and salaries. The value of savings -will be materially lessened. The result would- be hardship to nearly every one, and hardship in very unequal measure.
It is scarcely necessary for me to say that a rising cost of living is a source of acute personal anxiety to all and, particularly, to those with small incomes. And it is -this very anxiety which is the danger to our war effort. For in the making of war no weapon is more powerful than peace of mind. We all know -that we cannot do our best work and put forth our utmost effort if we are beset by personal fears and anxieties. And we know- that a maximum war effort for Canada depends upon each and all working together in conditions that are just to all. That is why the government which is responsible for the direction of Canada's war effort is deeply concerned about the effect of rapidly rising prices upon the prosecution of the war. That is why the government has decided that hereafter prices must be controlled more rigorously than they have been during the first two years of war. The needs- of today demand it.
I submit that if the situation in Canada in October, 1941, warranted that sort of speech, the situation in Canada in February, 194S, deserves action far different from the appointment of a parliamentary committee-simplytrying to transfer the responsibility to sixteen members of this house who are in no way responsible for formulating policy and are denied the power of making recommendations after they have discovered the facts. The Prime Minister in that speech emphasized the danger of inflation, and I submit that if the government was serious about inflation in those days it should certainly- be facing up to the problem now. I have here a pamphlet, "I lived through an inflation", by- Hans Habe, issued by the wartime prices and trade board. The writer tells of his experiences in Germany and says:
In December, 1921, wholesale prices were on the average thirty-five times higher than the year before the war. One year later, prices were 1.500 times as high. Two years later, at Christmas. 1923, they were 1,262,000,000 times higher than pre-war prices.
The writer goes -on to give some of his personal experiences. He mentions that Arthur Edel, who owned a good stock of German and French wines, instead of selling them wholesale began to sell them by the bottle when inflation came. In 1921 the price of a bottle of Veuve Clicquot-I shall have to get some of my friends to help me with the pronunciation-was 40 marks. In December, 1923, Arthur Edel got 3,000,000,000 marks for the same bottle of champagne.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: It was a lot older then.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: This German dealer had a fairly good supply. But he gave up selling those bottles at three billion marks each because three billion marks would not buy him a loaf of bread. He made a trip across to Holland and found that a bottle brought $4 in good United States money in Rotterdam. He came back across the line with his dollars in his shoes and could have disposed of his S4 for a few billion marks, but he did not. He kept his dollars safely until he had 250 of them altogether. Then he went out and bought the finest house in Berlin, with a very expensive Rembrandt thrown in.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: Does the hon. member advocate trafficking in wine?

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
If the hon. member would listen to me he would know that I am not advocating trafficking in wine. I am talking about inflation. Here is the story of Rudolf Bauer. Rudolf and his brother inherited the equivalent of about $10,000 each when their father died. Rudolf was an accountant and was very thrifty. Like thrifty people, he put his money away in safe-keeping. The brother was not so thrifty. He enjoyed wine, beer, and other strong drinks and his money- was soon spent. When Rudolf realized finally- what inflation was doing to his country
Prices Committee

he decided he had better get his $10,000 and have a little fun with it. When he got his money he was not able to buy a postage stamp to send a letter to his brother. But the brother who was so reckless with his money had a hobby of collecting wine bottles. He disposed1 of his empty wine bottles for several billion marks. These are stories published] by the government of Canada to enlist the co-operation of the citizens of this country when we were fighting for our very lives. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) and I happened to be in Europe during those chaotic times, and we know something of the demoralizing effect it has on a community when the savings of a lifetime will not purchase a postage stamp. The writer says:
When inflation suddenly came to an end, everyone frantically sought a way back to normal life, but the way was barred. The moral chaos which had been created proved an insurmountable obstacle. During the period of madness rapid enrichment and sudden impoverishment became common phenomena. Hard work, achievement, effort, lost their good name. The poor became rich and the rich poor.
It was these chaotic conditions in Germany that made it possible for a madman like Hitler to capture the imagination of people who were committing suicide by the thousands. According to the writer of this article, four million people in Germany died of starvation or suicide during this critical period. I submit to the government of Canada that if this pamphlet was worth printing in 1942 it is worth paying some attention to by the people who are responsible for the affairs of Canada now.
I want to go back to what I said earlier, that the cabinet of Canada is completely out of touch with public opinion in the country at the present time. On the front page of today's Toronto Daily Star we find the following :
Crash inevitable if price rise not halted-* Truman.
President Truman said today prices are rising so alarmingly that a crash is inevitable unless something is done to halt them.
Poor President Truman is in the position of having no legislation, no power to act. Here in Canada we have the legislation on our statute books; we have public support for action. Instead of action the government of Canada is recommending a committee that will meet for weeks and months and then will not have an opportunity to report.
Again in the Toronto Daily Star of Tuesday, February 3, there appears a picture at the top of which appears the following:
These are hungry jobless lined up for meal in Toronto.

Toronto the good; not China; not India; not Africa; in Toronto in February, 1948. Underneath the picture appears the following:
Free meal tickets donated by an unknown Bay street financier were the target of almost five hundred unemployed Toronto men who lined up at King and Market streets yesterday. Three hundred pasteboards entitling holders to a meal were given out and this will be duplicated every day until end of March. Scene recalls days of 1933 when hunger lines were common.
The following appears in the Ottawa Journal of January 31;
Lack of funds forces veterans to leave Carle-ton college.
At least two student veterans have been forced to leave Carleton college for lack of funds to carry on their courses. Four others who left at Christmas are believed to have given up for the same reason.
I am glad the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) is listening. I am sure he is in sympathy with these young men who have been forced to discontinue their studies. Here is the case of Lome. Ruddy as told to the Journal. Hon. members may laugh at a student veteran in Carleton college being denied the right to complete his education, but I wrant to tell my hon. friends that this young man served as a navigator in Canada during the war. He was trained at the expense of the Canadian people to the extent of $28,000. I think it is disgraceful that any man, who served his country as gallantly as the men in the army, air force and navy did, should be told that because of the rising cost of living, because this government fails to act, he cannot complete his education.
Mr. GIBSON (Comox-Alberni); I think the minister is going to do something about it.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
The article goes on to say:
Representatives of student veterans in universities across Canada met during the Christmas holidays and prepared a brief asking for a cost of living bonus to supplement the basic $60 a month education allowances. The brief will be presented to the veterans affairs parliamentary committee this session.
What the brief asks for is a five per cent increase for every six points rise in the cost of living index from October, 1944. At the December index this would give the single veteran, now receiving $60 about $73.50, and the married veteran without children, now receiving $80, about $98.
I am sure that the Minister of Veterans Affairs cannot be satisfied with the treatment that Canada is giving to her student veterans.
In the last edition of Veterans Affairs, published at Ottawa twice monthly by authority

Prices Committee
of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, we find a picture on page 4 with the following underneath :
Melbourne W. Prime, VLA full-time farmer on 124 acres at Rossway, Digb.v county, Nova Scotia, is here shown posing with his team of young oxen outside his barn. Fine teams of oxen are quite common in the Digby area, and they do a lot of work for their owners. They are later sold for beef at a good profit.
I submit that the buying of oxen for our Canadian veterans is not just good enough in the year 1948. The nation that could spend $25,000 to train pilots, $27,000 to train observers, and 828,000 to train navigators can certainly do something to see that these young people are permitted to complete their university education. Many of them went into the forces right out of high school. Who can estimate what the contribution that this young chap, whose name is mentioned in the paper, might make to us in ten years time? He wanted to be a chemist. Others want to be architects, engineers, and so on. They want to enter into our Canadian economy and make some useful contribution.
I have other clippings from the newspapers. One says:
One hundred per cent butter profit.
Price paid farmers from 35 to 37 cents.
Butter which cost 40 cents last July is now being retailed at 73 cents.
Another clipping says:
Cabbage ceiling set at nine cents by prices board.
Well, we are having rationing now. It is not the customary coupon rationing we had during the war. We are having rationing so that those who have money can buy cabbage at nine cents a pound, while those who are depending on a worker's cheque just have to go without.
From the Montreal Gazette of Thursday, January 29, 1948, I read:
A C.C.F. government resolution calling for reimposition of price controls on all goods of primary necessity and the re-establishment of subsidies was passed by a substantial majority at the Model parliament held at McGill university last night with national and provincial figures leading the various parties.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) and the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Lesage) were three speakers from parliament. I think it is significant that in Montreal a majority, out of 500 students of McGill, would support a resolution of that sort, in a province where there is not supposed to be much support for such views.
During debates on problems of this kind there have been references to the claim that members of the C.C.F. are out for controls because we want to push people around. There is no truth in that claim. We have no desire to pry into other people's business and to ask them to do what is unreasonable. Our reason for supporting controls and subsidies is that they have worked. The majority of the Canadian people know that there were some irregularities and some hardships, but we were able during the war years to distribute the goods available in Canada more fairly than ever before in the history of the country. I represent a very large constituency spread over an area of 112 miles east and west and 500 miles north and south, and my opinion is that if it had not been for rationing and controls the storekeepers throughout the constituency would have found it impossible to get their supplies of sugar, overalls, stockings, cereals and other commodities which were in short supply. While there were difficulties, most fair-minded people will, I believe, agree that the wartime prices and trade board did a reasonably good job, and I submit that in modern civilization we shall have to accept more and more controls. When my grandfather built his log house in Bruce county there were no building restrictions that determined how he should build; but if he were to build in Ottawa today he could not object to having civic regulations stipulating that the house should be built according to certain standards, so that if the fire brigade were called a fireman would not lose his life by falling through a roof that had not been built to support him. In a well organized society we accept building restrictions because they are for the common good.
In one of the Ottawa papers of January 23 I read of a winter hotel at Ste. Marguerite, Quebec, having been destroyed by fire, a hotel that cost over $600,000. What was that hotel for? Was it for veterans of the war? Was it for old people in Quebec who have worked so hard to produce food and other commodities? No; it was for the skiers.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: It was for everybody.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
No. It was for people who want to go into that beautiful part of the world for a holiday, and in normal times it is all right for people to have holidays in such lodges. But it is not in the interests of the public, when building materials are short, when carpenters are in demand everywhere, to put up a building of this kind costing $600,000 in the Laurentians for a few rich people who want to have holidays there, win-
Prices Committee

ter and summer, especially when there are so many veterans in Canada who have not yet been able to get homes for themselves.
In concluding my remarks I wish to say as emphatically as I can that the problem facing Canada is not a problem for fifteen private members of the house and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to undertake. If the government of Canada do not know what is causing the rise in prices, and are not prepared to take the necessary action to deal with it, let them say so and resign.
I realize that at the moment the leader of this party would not be able to get a majority of the house to support the views which he and members of this group have submitted from time to time. We accept that as democracy. But I wish to say that if our views are not acceptable it is the responsibility of the government to pull a trick out of the bag and demonstrate that it can work.
The leader of this party outlined the solutions as we understand them:
1.	The reimposition at the earliest possible date of price controls on all basic necessities of life: food, clothing and fuel.
2.	The renewal of subsidies on milk, butter, bread, feed grains, cotton and wool.
3.	The closing of the Winnipeg grain exchange and the elimination of all speculation in foods.
4.	The reconstruction of the wartime prices and trade board in such a manner that it can adequately administer price controls.
5.	The continuation of the excess profits tax after December 31, 1947.
6.	Rationing, if necessary, of any essential commodity which is in short supply, so that all Canadians may get their reasonable share.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
I have listened to this debate and I wish to make a few remarks. I have taken some notes. First of all, let me say that I am in favour of this committee, not because I necessarily agree with the policy of the government or otherwise; but if it is to be a fact-finding committee, and I take it there is a genuine desire that it shall be a fact-finding committee, then I am in favour of it because I think, if there is one thing we are all in need of, it is facts. That applies to the members of the house just as much as it does to the general public.
While I am, of course, perfectly willing to grant that every member is anxious to improve the standard of living in this country, I cannot avoid coming to the conclusion, after

listening to some of the speeches, especially from the C.C.F., that some do not want facts, and that is why they do not want a committee.
We hear that price control is the cure-all. We are told that everybody wants control. I do not believe it. What people want is a lower cost of Living, and that is not the same thing as control. I know it has been argued that present high prices are due to the removal of controls. It seems to me that is the sort of argument which might be used when, after the waterpipes are frozen, when the thaw comes, one gets the flood, and people who do not stop to think might assume that the thaw is the cause of the burst pipes; whereas we all know that the freezing burst the pipes and we get the result of it only when the thaw comes. I think that analogy can be used with regard to these controls. I think the freezing of our economy under control was the real cause of what we are suffering from today, but we might not notice t'he evil results of it until the controls are unfrozen.
As I said before, I assume, of course, that a genuine use will be made of the committee for the purpose of arriving at the facts and that nothing will 'be hidden that could possibly be of use. First of all, I should like to say that price control must include wage control. 'When the people to. whom I have talked demand control, it is always the control of other people and of what the other people have to sell. The person who wants control does not want control of his own products or labour. As I say, labour will have to realize that, in. order to control prices, wages must be controlled; for, in order that prices may be lowered, wages must be lowered. I can see no argument against that.
When we talk about high prices, we mean that they are high in relation to what-in relation to prices in the depression of fifteen years ago? Do we not really mean that prices are high in. relation to income? That is what people mean when they say that prices are high; they mean that they are too high for people's income. So, instead of imposing controls, it might be argued, why not raise the income of the people to meet the higher prices? Why must we deflate and go through all the misery of deflation? Is it a fact that reducing prices will bring about the results that we all desire? I very well remember the situation fifteen years ago during the deflation when, prices were lower than they had ever before been known to be. Surely nobody in this house will contradict me when I say that at that time, with the lowest prices in history, we had the greatest amount of misery in the

Prices Committee
country that we had ever known, far greater than we know today. That is one argument against the idea that, by lowering prices the living standards of the people will automatically be increased.
When people say they want control, what do they really mean? Day in and day out, over the radio and by speakers everywhere there has been dinned into their heads the idea that what they want is control, control, control. Why do we not tell them that what they really want is to be enabled to buy the things they want to buy. That is what they really want. They do not want controls. They did not want them during the war. I had plenty of people tell me that and tell me to do what I could to remove the controls we had; because, as I shall show later, the fact that we are suffering from high prices today is not fundamentally a condition brought about by the removal of controls; at least, in my opinion it is not. There are many causes for it.
Of course the buyers want lower prices, but the sellers want higher prices. For instance, this week I have had some petitions with regard to margarine. I am told to use all the pressure I can bring to bear to prevent the manufacture and importation of margarine. What is the purpose of that policy if it is not to keep up the price of butter? I do not know what other reason there could be for it. Margarine is not unwholesome; I am not saying that it is as good as butter, but it is not unwholesome. Why, then, should people demand that the sale of margarine be prohibited? The only reason I can think of is that those who are interested in the dairy business want to keep up the price of butter and they are afraid that with the removal of the prohibition against margarine, the price of butter would fall. I do not know of any other reason.
Labour, of course, now wants higher wages, but higher wages mean higher prices while lower prices mean lower wages. I do not think there should be any dispute about those statements. If you are to have control of prices you must have control of wages, and one control leads on to another until you have nothing but control. That, I think, is the aim and end of Marxian socialism.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: You have applied it in Alberta in controlling the press.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
I cannot see that those
countries which are under Marxian socialism furnish any useful pattern for us to follow. I myself believe, as I think everyone else does who is willing to admit it, that, as far as living conditions go, we in Canada are as well
off as, and probably better off than, any other people on earth. I think that is a commonplace. I cannot see any country under control that can be put forward by anybody as an example for us to follow. Rather I think it should be an example for us to avoid.
We in this group have been here for thirteen years. It is a long time, and we have consistently advocated an economic policy which has, so far, fallen on deaf ears. But before sitting down I should like to quote a report made by the Southampton chamber of commerce in Great Britain. They held an inquiry into the economic conditions which existed in 1932, and appointed a committee which went to the root of the matter. It was a fact-finding committee, as I hope this one will be. That is why I am voting for it. If I thought otherwise I would vote against it.
They issued their report, and that report has now run into thirteen editions. I shall quote briefly from it because I believe it goes to the root of the trouble. This is the statement of the president of the Southampton chamber of commerce in October, 1947. In the course of his remarks he said:
From January of 1933 to June of the same year this special committee of ours pursued its trying and onerous task, and eventually published a report, known as the economic crisis committee's report. Fifteen editions of this report have been published in this country alone, and it still enjoys a worldwide circulation.
It constitutes a searching analysis of the existing financial and economic system, and discloses the flaw which for over 100 years has denied to the population the fulfilment of their natural desires. It further reveals that ever since the advent of the machine age the old money-making mechanism has been unable to eject sufficient purchasing power to enable the public to acquire the goods which the machine can so freely produce.
That was the Southampton chamber of commerce. Then he goes on to say:
Significantly enough, the London chamber of commerce working as I have already said, quite independently, arrived at a conclusion similar to our own.
And later on:
Let me add this. In the spring of 1942, the Association of British Chambers of Commerce itself appointed a special committee to consider post-war economic reconstruction, the findings of this committee coinciding, in effect, with those of the London and Southampton chambers. The aim, said the Association of British Chambers of Commerce report, must be to equate production with consumption, and not, as in the past, to restrict production to the consuming power available.
To crown all, one of the major declarations at the Hot Springs conference was to the following effect:	"Never in the world's history has
Prices Committee

a sufficiency of purchasing power been issued to the people of the world to enable them to consume what they can produce."
And finally he said:
Thus I am brought 'to my first point which is: that the paramount and primary duty which devolved upon the government was, and is, that of adjusting the money system as advocated in the three reports I have mentioned. Only by so doing can effect be given to the economic law: "Consumption is the sole end, the crown, of production."
There you have the opinion, not only of the Southampton chamber of commerce, whose report has stood the test of time for fifteen years, but that of the London chamber of commerce, the British Association of Chambers of Commerce and the Hot Springs conference of the United States. All are agreed that the fundamental trouble is to be found with the existing financial system.
I have no hesitation in saying that we must make the choice now between an adjustment in the financial system, so that we may retain all the benefits we enjoy, and submitting to an ever-increasing control which will end up in one frozen hell of controls.
Before we find a permanent solution we must have the facts, and it is my hope that the facts will be found; that they will be examined, and not hidden. That is why I shall vote for the committee.
Meantime for many people in the country there is what may be described as a state of emergency. People in low-income brackets, people on fixed incomes, pensioners of all kinds, those who are living on past savings and, of course, the lower paid people such as stenographers, are vitally affected. Girls are working faithfully today for $80 a month; how can they possibly live on salaries such as that and keep themselves looking smart, as they have to do, and at the same time enjoy a reasonable standard of living? For those people something has to be done, and done immediately. For them it is an emergency. There is no reason in the world why we cannot bonus those people; and I do not care what it is called, if you do not like the word "bonus". Call it a cost of living allowance, if you wish. But I say we in the House of Commons have the responsibility of putting an end to their suffering; because it is suffering, and cannot be called anything else under existing conditions.
Therefore, while I vote for the committee, in the hope that it will be a genuine factfinding committee, at the same time I implore the government to do something; indeed, to do more than something, to do the right thing by these unfortunate people who are caught by this rise in the cost of living.

The cost of living, which has reached a fantastic level, is causing deep concern to governments and individuals. The statements made in good faith, the predictions voiced time and again, the hopes entertained that the cost of living, after reaching a certain level, would remain stationary, have been an utter disappointment. In the United States, prices have risen in a most alarming way; the situation there, involving a threat of inflation which will soon materialize, has repercussions in this country. Even admitting that the cost of living is perhaps lower here than anywhere else, we must however acknowledge that it cannot continue to rise without causing violent reactions within Canada.
During the war, I have sometimes criticized controls in this house. It was not so much because of their underlying principle, for they have prevented a repetition of the glaring abuses of the first world war, but because of the bureaucracy which they brought into being, and whose zeal, often exaggerated, and in certain cases smacking of petty politics, lowered the prestige not only of the Board but also of the government which, standing above petty politics, aimed solely at serving the people.

War came to an end. The public demanded the abolition of controls-which had been established only for the duration of the war-because the conflict was over, because they were, it was said, encouraging the black market. Controls, we might as well frankly admit it, had had the direct and beneficial effect of ensuring the proper distribution of food and the necessaries of life, making them available to all members of the community whatever might have been their calling and their station in life, and at prices which, without being necessarily low, were at least reasonable. The black market was then in existence; it operated with prices

Prices Committee
that gave rise to justified grumblings and complaints. However, its dealings were conducted secretly with many precautions, a prudent hesitation and on a rather small scale. Today, we have the "white market" which operates openly with a disconcerting impudence and a boldness which goes so far as to challenge the law.
In my case, I have received hundreds upon hundreds of letters, cards or circulars demanding the burial of controls. After the war, the government, which had received thousands of them, saw fit to abolish controls gradually, to preserve freedom of trade, and democratic laws regarding competition. For a few months, prices hardly rose, then did rise in a normal and even legitimate way considering the difficulties of production, the scarcity of shipping, the lack of raw materials, increased manufacturing costs and the rise in salaries. But after removal of all or nearly all rationing measures, many speculators enforced their own controls upon the market.
Personally, I am against all peacetime controls. For the co-ordination of common efforts, I accept them in war time although war has often been an excuse for originating and multiplying them. If, normally, control should only exist in a democratic country, to play its part properly, democracy must nevertheless protect the weak against the greed of the strong, give the weak a fighting chance and curb the immoderate ambition of the strong. Let me say again that personally I am not in favour of peacetime controls, but if in peace time, certain cartels profiteer on the necessities of life, I feel the government has the right and more than the right to control. Profiteering must not be tolerated in Canada. In my opinion, there is, for example, in the agricultural field, too high a margin between the prices farmers receive for their products and those charged consumers after the product has passed through a series of middlemen and finally through some great concerns whose assets dominate and control.
We have laws enabling the government to investigate companies' business, scrutinize their books, apportion legitimate profits and extravagant revenues. The hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has specified that, if necessary, he would act in that sense. We can only approve this stand. It is proposed to set up a parliamentary committee to investigate into the rise in prices and to bring to light the combines of certain trusts. I approve of this committee. But if necessary
and if it is proven, even before the committee's report is tabled, that there have been or that there are now abuses let us at once apply the branding-iron. During the war, certain trusts, long known for their greed and inhumanity-a trust is soulless-could not make as much money as they wanted to. Cornered by controls, they were waiting for better circumstances. They want to make up for "lost" years, to take advantage of the scarcity of certain goods or raw materials, first to hoard them, then to control market prices according to their whims and wishes.
I repeat that, for my part, I shall support in this house all the legislation aimed directly at shielding the lower classes from the snares of big money and profiteering business concerns. If, because of circumstances beyond our control, price ceilings on various commodities must remain high, I think it would be fitting to inquire, through a parliamentary committee or otherwise, into the advisability of adjusting, on a fair basis, those salaries that are still way out of line with the cost of living, or even to reconsider the policy of granting subsidies temporarily, where required, and more especially in some particular cases. To my mind, on the other hand, just because of the increased cost of living, and more particularly if the government feels that it would be dangerous to return to a subsidizing policy even in a few restricted fields, it would be fitting to curtail substantially various hidden taxes, such as those on soft drinks and tobacco, to lower the postal rate, the sales tax on many daily needs, etc. Such reductions would slightly offset the increased cost of living. but for the same reason, let us not forget to effect a substantial cut with respect to income tax.
