speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reasons that would warrant this house in setting up a committee to investigate the high cost of living would surely warrant empowering that committee to bring

Prices Committee
in recommendations. If we cannot assume that, the whole proceeding is a farce from beginning to end. The cost of living is a vital issue at the present time, and I quite appreciate why the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), speaking this afternoon in his usual eloquent fashion, found it difficult to follow the party he loves so much. I realize that he probably has, of course, a still greater love for Spadina than for the Liberal policies of today. It was amusing to hear him giving his reasons why he opposed the ex-minister of finance, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), who had just told the house that the Liberal party was through with subsidies, and then to hear such a stalwart supporter of the party as the hon. member for Spadina embrace subsidies as the solution of the high cost of living.
There are important factors which might well have been brought to the attention of the committee and which have some bearing on the high cost of living if the scope of the committee had been made as wide as is usual with investigating committees. I am as sympathetic as anyone toward those on whom the burden of the present high cost of living falls most heavily. I know a great many industrial workers just as the hon. member for Spadina does in the industrial sections of his riding, and I know it is difficult for these men who are working on hourly rates, despite any increase there may have been in those rates, to meet the present costs of living. I know it is difficult too for the white-collared men, the clerks and the girls working in offices and stores, and people generally who live on small incomes.
Similar difficulties, though not to the same degree, were experienced by those living on small incomes following world war I. I can well remember at that time, when I first had anything to do with politics, how the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1920 and 1921 on every platform from which he spoke from coast to coast denounced the high cost of living which he said had been brought about by the government that had been in power during the war. That was his main topic, and it was one topic on which he made the same speech in the west as he did in the east. He emphasized that the cost of living was a vital factor in the welfare and happiness of the lives of the common people and that unless we eased this terrific burden on those living on small incomes we should strangle trade. I remember how he said that one of the chief reasons for the high cost of living was high taxation and he urged that certain taxes be removed. He criticized the
party which now sits to your left, Mr. Speaker, for having had a protective policy and for having imposed tariffs on the tools of production and promised that if his party was elected that protection would be removed. He also cited excise taxes as another vicious type of taxation which increased the cost of living. Yet only a few weeks ago his government by order in council increased excise taxes by twenty-five per cent.
The ex-minister of finance this afternoon twitted those of us on this side of the house with having different opinions. He said that one of our members believed that the sales tax was justified, while another member was not so sure that it was. That indicates that there is independence of thought on this side of the house.
When the sales tax was one per cent I remember the present Prime Minister raising his voice in holy horror at that tax and demanding its removal because, he said, it was increasing the cost of living. I remember when the sales tax in the days of the Bennett government had, over the years, been gradually raised from one per cent to two,, three, four and finally six per cent; and in 1935, during the election campaign the present Prime Minister and his cohorts, some of them now in the cabinet, declared that they would remove the sales tax if they were returned to power. But what happened? They were returned to power, and the very first year they were in power, in 1936, they raised the sales tax to eight per cent. Similarly the Prime Minister denounced the high protection policies of the previous government. Today we find that the Liberal government has not only increased the sales tax to the highest point it has ever been but has introduced protective and well-nigh prohibitive policies in many respects.
There are other factors that enter into the cost of living. I have listened with sympathy to hon. members to my left just as I did to the hon. member for Spadina this afternoon. There is no one in the world who is not concerned about the high cost of living and also about the shortages of foodstuffs, which are at the root of the increased cost of living. When one realizes that children overseas are starving for the want of food it is obvious that something must be done. I believe all hon. members read the speech made by that delightful Canadian girl, Miss Mary Pickford. In that speech she asked for assistance for the children of Europe. What are we doing in Canada? What has been the policy of this government? What have they done to create the surplus that is needed?
Prices Committee

I have every sympathy for what was said this afternoon by an hon. member. It was difficult for him to say it; it took some courage to say it, especially when he was surrounded by those with whom he finds himself associated. If he believes that the way to do it is by controls he is welcome to his opinion. I believe it is his honest opinion; but we find that we have had a government that has started in with controls, and it has made one error in one control. Then it created another error in bringing on another control to control the first control or to decontrol.
We find that the United States of America has been criticized repeatedly by those who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker. They were criticized by the ex-minister of finance a year or so ago because of inflation, inflation that might be brought about by the relinquishing of control. We have a government that has built up such a bureaucracy they want to hang on to all the controls necessary in time of war so that they can enjoy them in time of peace. What has happened? If these champions of the control system could show you tonight that we had increased production all along the line and that the reason for the high cost of living was that we were sending so much to Europe to feed the starving people who must be taken care of, there might be some justification for it. That is not so. We find ourselves in the position tonight of having in Canada today scarcely more than one-third of the number of hogs on the farms that we had in the midst of the war when our boys were overseas and the farmers could not get enough labour to carry on. Today we find the lumber camps filling up. Today construction men are more plentiful. Today there are some signs of unemployment in certain places; yet we find there is only about one-third of the hogs to look after in the wintertime when such seasonal work is not so plentiful.
What does that mean to the children of Europe? What does it mean to the British housewife who has four or five children between fourteen and twenty years of age, that growing age when they need more meat? Today in Great Britain we find the bacon is so thin that one would think it was cut with a safety razor blade. That is done in order to string it out. I just forget at the moment what the ration is, but I believe it has been an ounce or two a week for a long time.
Not long ago I was in England, but I did not suffer very much. I met the former Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) over there and I think he felt the same way as I did. He did not seem to be suffering much more than I did. He must have
[Mr. Rowe.)
felt guilty, as I did, in eating plentifully as we did at some of the hotels and observing such shortages at other places that we visited. What will it mean to the people of Great Britain? Hon. members may ask, why is it that our production has fallen off? Check back on the Canada Year Books and find out what happened in 1918, 1919 and 1920. To the champions of control and those who state that the government of that day had raised the cost of living, I say that they received their answer this afternoon in the speech delivered by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). I am not going to burden the house further with a repetition of it. I think the hon. member for Souris this afternoon showed quite clearly that the cost of living, percentagewise, is almost fifty per cent higher now than it was in 1920.
I can well remember being in stockyards out in the rural districts of the county that I now represent and seeing farmers coming in to market with loads of hogs. I can well remember their taking back a load that was not quite finished. If the farmer was short of grain and had no money to buy grain the hogs never went to market. They were taken out of his load, put on another man's load and taken home. One dealer told me that during the whole year of 1921 or 1922-I just cannot recall which year following the last war-he had not shipped one hog to the market in six months that did not weigh over 200 pounds, because the price was high enough to warrant feeding them. Conditions were such that there was sufficient profit to encourage the farmer to take the hogs home and put another fifty pounds on them. Fifty pounds more on a hog would feed a lot of people. If you put fifty pounds each on a million hogs today it would amount to a lot of meat.
Is it realized that the meat production of this country last year was scarcely over fifty per cent what it was in the mid-war years with all the shortage of labour? These are some of the fundamental reasons for our difficulties, and it is time we stopped, looked and listened. It is time we called a halt. Is it a case of not enough controls, or it is because of this control system and this new socialized agricultural policy that is falling down around our ears, that we have a shortage in our midst? Can you tell me, Mr. Speaker, that you can take from one class of people in this dominion and gamble with their products in that greatest, most hectic and largest gamble ever made with our products in the history of our country, which has been done by the Department of Agriculture? I am not going to go into that at the present time. I see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is in the chamber. I heard him speak the other evening. I was

Prices Committee
delighted, because I like the Minister of Agriculture; but my heart almost bled for him the other night when I read that in one of these agricultural meetings the farmers booed such a little champion of agricultural interests as he is. They booed him in one place; they booed him in another place; but he fought gallantly, as he is capable of doing. I was delighted, and I know everyone in this House of Commons was pleased to note that he has still one friend at each conference who can write him a letter to read in the house.

However, I find that percentagewise during the last year the cost of living in Canada has increased twice as much as it has in the United States of America.
I have made general references to our meat situation. The same is true with reference to eggs. Everybody knows that. The Minister of Agriculture knows the story, if nobody else does. I think he knows it better than most people. I know I have lost some money on a thousand laying hens. Cheese is in just about the same plight. No one has worried more about it than the Minister of Agriculture; at least no one should worry more about it. It is half as much as it was in the mid-war years. I hope I am not over-emphasizing this, Mr. Speaker, but I trust you are grasping the significance of it. In the midst of the war, with the shortage of help, equipment rationed, young men overseas, and so on, it was difficult to produce. Today our young men have come back and are trying to start farming. Munitions factories in the district took young men who, in time of peace, would have been at home to look after the livestock. The old folks had to work long into the night. The
boys were down at the Malton airport or in the factories around Toronto. Today as I have said in the house repeatedly-and I know the Minister of Agriculture agrees with me in this; I know he has the same purpose in mind as I have, although he has such devious means to achieve it; he knows as well as I do; we have both said it in the house repeatedly -that food won the war. Food will win the peace. There is nothing more important than food today.
The greatest feature of the present economic crisis is the worldwide shortage of food. The hon. member for Spadina said this glibly this afternoon when warning my hon. friends to the left about being too closely associated with those who are sympathetic with other powers. If we are to maintain our place in the sun; if we are to maintain our place in this war that is still going on, whether a cold war or a hot war, we must see that food is provided. Many of us are thinking in common in that respect, andi for the next three years food) will be the most vital factor in peace, more vital than bullets were in the war. Yet what are we in Canada, with the greatest wealth per capita of any country, with magnificent agricultural	lands-this
country is known as the bread-basket of the world-with greater resources than any similar number of people in the worldl have ever enjoyed-doing with all our wealth and our resources?
If we continue to reduce production steadily as we have been doing in the last year or two we shall have a sorry story to tell our children and our children's children of the part that we have played in this most crucial time in our history. To me it is amazing that some of these things are not to be brought before the committee. I repeat, the very factors that warrant this house in appointing a committee are factors which are strong enough to warrant- that committee in bringing a recommendation to- parliament, and if the committee does not do that, then it will be a farce.
The whole situation is bleak and barren in many ways; and I have never seen a more bleak, more barren and empty proposal submitted to parliament than the proposal for the setting up of the committee in this way. Will this committee be empowered to bring before it officials of the combines investigation commission? Will it be empowered to bring before it the enforcement branch of the wartime prices and trade board? No one says, yes. I wish someone would. Even if the Minister of Agriculture, from where he is at present sitting at the back, would say yes, or even nod his head, I would be satisfied. But
Prices Committee

no. There is nothing but silence. As the government study the error of their ways they have nothing but silent remorse and regret for the mess they have created.
What happened on September 19? That is five months ago. What did the Toronto Star have to say? I know the Minister of Agriculture never doubts them because they rarely doubt him; and I see an item, which is a special to the Star, stating that Ottawa will keep prices down by exposing profiteers. This is stated to be Ottawa's program. I quote:
Government rearguard action-
It has been mostly rearguard.
-against undue price increases in the wake of decontrol is being launched here through the wartime prices and trade board, and the combines investigation commission, official sources disclosed today.
The program is designed to "scare" business against unjustified price boosts by two methods:	threat of investigation and exposure
where a combine in restraint of trade is suspected, and the release of information to the public indicating just what price increases are justifiable.
Those are the two techniques that are to be used and they believe this will work. Well, bread was raised only three cents in Montreal, but it was raised five cents in Winnipeg. Of course they may not have secured the news out there. The western people seem to be brave.
Will any member of the government rise in his place and tell me that this committee will take action to deal with these matters? That is five months ago. We had a short session last fall but we did not hear about this. This was government policy. The Toronto Star had printed the story; and men were shaking and shivering in Toronto because they were fearful of the cracking down of the wartime prices and trade board, fearful of the combines investigation commission, fearful of the hand of the King government, even so long before an election. They were afraid that something might be done, but not a thing was done.
Will someone tell us that this committee will be given further powers to carry out this scare policy? Will anyone tell me that they will be allowed to go as far as that?
In the mellowness of his years, the Prime Minister said the other day that there are greedy men, mean men, men who will do terrible things, who will almost take the food away from crying children whose parents have to pay so much. He knows all that, and so does the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), another heir-apparent, though perhaps by the time the leadership becomes an issue, no one will want that crown

so badly. The minister of external affairs, speaking in Montreal not long ago, had this to say:
The repercussions of the efforts of everyone to maintain or improve his standard in the distribution of the nation's aggregate revenue lights a new trend of the same powder. . . . But this provides the greedy-and unfortunately they exist everywhere and always-the opportunity to find exorbitant profit cuts. It is necessary to find means to bring them to reason . . . We know it and we are working on it.
The other day the Prime Minister said he was aware that there were these greedy people, these profiteers, and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) declared that profiteering would end. He knows them and the minister of external affairs knows them.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
We have the wartime prices and trade board; and all I am asking is that some member of the cabinet will rise or even nod his head to indicate that the government will consider asking these men from the wartime prices and trade board and from the combines investigation commission, who have been running around the country frightening these people for a long time, to tell us now how they frighten them. There are many things that happen that we do not know about. There are orders in council that we do not see except when we read of them in the Toronto Star. That has a large circulation and the news looks the same in it as in the Globe and Mail. But we see it there first, and it is not surprising that some cabinet ministers come here and learn about orders in council that they did not know had been passed.
This order went out on September 19. The cost of living was rising faster than at any previous time in the history of the country, and we had a short session of parliament, but we did not hear about these greedy fellows. The Prime Minister says now that the greedy fellows are around. Were they not around last summer? Have they just come into the country? Let me quote what the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 747 of Hansard'.
The people of this country want to have their representatives in this parliament proceed to discover the causes underlying what they have experienced thus far of what they believe to be an unwarranted rise in prices, whether due to profiteering, hoarding, or any other cause.

Prices Committee
But in clause (c) he makes sure that the committee does not go too far. First, the committee is to inquire into the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living. -It must be recent. He would not even remove the word "recent", because apparently it has started only recently. The committee is to investigate rises in prices due to the acquiring, accumulating or withholding from sale by any persons, firms or corporations of any goods beyond amounts reasonably required for the ordinary purposes of their businesses. That is all the power that the committee will have. If there are greedy people and the government knew about them all along, why n.ot widen the terms of the investigation? The right hon. gentleman said further down on the same page of Hansard:
The committee is not intended to be a prosecuting tribunal; it is hoped it may save the need for prosecutions. The committee is a fact-finding body. Its purpose is the publicizing of facts, not the prosecution of offenders.
He says further that, once the facts are known, he has every confidence in the supremacy of parliament, that parliament may some day do something. He believes there is no way of combating crime like publicizing it; publicize it and let the people know, and the fellow will feel ashamed of himself. If that does not do it, he has confidence that parliament will some day do something. It must be a wonderful thing to be such a close follower of public sentiment that people almost assume that you are leading it.
What would happen if we set up every committee like this? Why all this scheming? Why not make it clear? Why do some of the cabinet not come out from under the table and tell us something of what they are thinking? I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce and how it must hurt him terribly to see a restraint like this, when the people are suffering-

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: He is crying.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
He is not minister of trade and commerce now, I know; he is Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacKinnon). I am glad that my genial friend is relieved of that burden. I shall not comment on how he fulfilled his position, but I must say that he is probably the happiest-looking man under difficulties in the present government.
The committee on banking and commerce have been sitting for many years. If they never recommended anything, why would they sit? As hon. members know, every ten years that committee amended the Bank Act. They brought in recommendations. We have other committees such as the radio committee. I well remember when, in 1935, I think it was,
the radio committee was set up. If it had
been so strangled and stifled and made barren before it started, what would have happened then? No, Mr. Speaker, the radio committee had some teeth in it. It changed the whole system. It recommended that there should be the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It did more than that. It kicked out all the other fellows who were on the board for fear that some of them might not have the right knowledge of radio, or of what should go over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, or that some of them might have been friends of the Bennett government. So they were removed.
There were many other committees. We have the veterans affairs committee; and how well I can remember-and I know you will recall it too, Mr. Speaker-how the genial Scotch ex-minister of veterans affairs spoke of it. We miss him in this house, and I hope he has long years of enjoyment in the other house; I know that his genial personality and his Scotch wit will amuse that house as it often entertained this one. I know he will be missed by the government, because in many respects he had better judgment than those he left. I well recall how, on repeated occasions, when he was telling what the members of the veterans affairs committee did, he praised all those men, such as the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) and others who were veterans, for the grand work they did. I could not help but admire his attitude when he mentioned that matter in the house, and said that the government could not claim all the credit for this veterans charter which was drawn up. He said he wanted to give credit where it was due, and the credit was due to those excellent veterans who sat on that committee and brought into being this veterans charter. What a contrast is this committee! Now we have this proposal, which is an insult to this house.
We also have the Indian affairs committee. Will that committee be restrained and restricted like this one. or will they bring in recommendation? Or will it be just a matter of publicity? We have the industrial relations committee also. What is the real reason underneath it all?
I could read what was said from 1920 on, but I have listened to it for so many years that I have not the heart to read it again. The present Prime Minister, back in 1920 and 1921, spoke about how the government should take the responsibility, that they had no policy with reference to the high cost of living; that it was their responsibility to remove the excise tax, to remove duties, remove taxes all along the line and cut out profiteering-the very thing that it is now his responsibility to do. But the reason that this committee is as barren
Prices Committee

as it is tonight is that this government has no policy on prices and no cost-of-living policy; it wants to restrain, restrict, gag and stifle the committee to make sure that nobody on it will give the government a lead as to how to find a policy. The government will flounder around; and, as was so well said this afternoon, this can go on for months. There are not many issues that, by the order of reference, can be discussed; but we do not know yet whether we can discuss, while parliament is sitting, the issues which are being discussed on this committee. Probably the Minister of Agriculture would nod his head, yes, to that. I imagine he does not know either.

speechtext:
He certainly is not interrupting. I realize that it is always easier for some men to have their mental faculties handier when they are sitting down than if they are on their feet.
I am not going to detain the house longer, because I think my hon. friends down here in Little Chicago want to catch the train to Montreal. I notice that even the leading papers in the country do not announce their absence as they announce ours; and I take that as a compliment, because when we are out of the house even the press misses us.
I should like to know if this is to be continued as government policy. It has not been government policy all through the years in the matter of setting up committees. The Prime Minister will probably tell us when he summarizes at the close of debate. I am sorry that he has entered the house just as I am about to resume my seat, because I would rather have spoken while he was here. I know that he is busier than I am, and he usually honours me by his presence. I may say to him that I would have even relieved him from listening to me at all, if some of his followers had not interrupted me so much. If they had followed that splendid parliamentary style he has practised for so many years they probably would not have interrupted so much today.
But I say in all seriousness that the Prime Minister might, when summarizing, tell us: Why all this discretion? Why all this fear?

Prices Committee
What is there to hide? Why not bring this issue out in the open and let us take a real look at it? Why so restrain us, and make this committee a mockery? The members of the committee will cease to function as members of parliament. They can do nothing but go out and find publicity, as the Prime 'Minister has said. It is nothing more or less than a sight-seeing expedition.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: Good.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Just a sight-seeing expedition. Someone says, "Good." Some people like to go on sight-seeing expeditions; but I never have gone on any sight-seeing trips which ever made me any money, or anything else. There are no recommendations to come from the committee, and I say that the Prime Minister should broaden the scope so that members from this side of the house may feel that they are sitting on a committee for some purpose.
I realize what was said this afternoon regarding boycotting the committee. I know the terrible furore which will go up from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) and the Prime Minister with respect to the supremacy of parliament. And he knows how to keep it supreme, and knows how to use it. It is supremely governed by his own party. I know he would say that we were breaking parliamentary rules if we did not sit on the committee. So, from the point of view of mockery it may be better to go in and sit on it. Certainly; maintain the dignity of this great House of Parliament.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: The Tories are good at that.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Better than your party is. And when you criticized us some years ago for passing orders in council, those orders in council did not hold parliament in the same contempt as yours have in the past few years. You talk about parliament today and compare it with what it was when we were in office. You criticize orders in council. The passing of orders in council has become almost a mockery, for in the quiet hours in the east block this government does more legislating than it does in parliament. And usually the press gets the report first.
I repeat that unless the powers of this committee are broadened so that they mean something, it will be of little use. I am not saying that members should not sit on it. I have not been asked to sit on it, but if I were I would feel I could not refuse. I know there are many others who could serve better than I could. But there is no use in anyone serving.
This is just a sight-seeing expedition started within the last five months from a statement in the Star, to frighten the people of this country, to publicize the government's own problem, and then to appoint a committee so that a solution could not be found. It might wind up like many other committees which had wider powers and which did not do much. However, no committee with such limited powers can do anything, but members will have to sit on it to preserve the dignity of parliament. But their effect and their status will be no more than gelded, fact-finding robots.
Mr. J. 0. PROBE (Regina City): Mr. Speaker, I feel I should be transgressing the rules as an elected' representative from my constituency, and in some measure as a representative of other electors in Canada, if I failed to rise this evening to add my voice to those who have spoken from all sides of the house against the ineffective form the present resolution has taken, so far as its impact on the cost of living is concerned. Were I not to speak, I would have failed to pay heed to the many communications, letters, telegrams and delegations I have received in the last few months. I know all other hon. members must have had a similar experience.
There is an overwhelming feeling in the country that the government will not do a job with respect to the important matter of living costs by investigating their causes in the manner suggested by the resolution of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The fact that up to this moment five cabinet ministers have spoken in defence of the government's policy is added evidence of the fact that they, too, are aware of the storm of public opinion, and that they are trying to adhere to the policy pronounced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) a year or so ago when he said that the policy of decontrol would be continued. The government is, of course, not so big in spirit that it will dare to admit it is wrong. Just today in the Ottawa Journal we read a press dispatch from Washington quoting no less a person than the President of the republic to the south of us, in which he admitted that the government there had made a mistake in connection with decontrol. The article is headed, "Prices too high, must be halted, President says". The American press of February 5, from Washington, has this to say in part:
President Truman said today prices are rising so alarmingly that a crash is inevitable unless something is done to halt them. For his part, Truman said, he will keep telling congress he needs authority to impose price controls.
Prices Committee

We intend1 to keep telling the Liberal government that it is high time they used the authority they now have to reimpose controls. There is no greater group of persons than those who, having made a mistake, will admit they have made it. I know pressure was on, immediately the war ended, to go on a rampage of collecting shekels which were available from those people who had thriftily done their duty during the war and had refrained from buying things they needed in their homes so that munitions of war could be bought instead.
I have here a little clipping which I presume has been paid for because it is published by the Canadian retail federation. It is a report on inflation and decontrol made to the Canadian retail federation oy J. L. McDougaM, associate professor of economics at Queen's university, on January 10, 1946. When I read this two years after it was delivered I do not doubt that the students of this associate professor of economics will seriously consider cutting his classes and going to some other fount of wisdom that comes nearer to being prophetic. I quote one short paragraph from page 15 as follows:
Nothing would do more today to increase production. and stabilize prices than a definite announcement from the government that it is intended) to remove price control completely, in the near future, and that, commencing at this moment, price control will be removed where-ever this is possible.
He predicted that with increased production we would stabilize prices. I have no doubt that production has been increased; but it has been hoarded, as the government seems to suspect by its announcement setting up this committee, or it has been disposed of in such a way that the consuming public have to use more and more of its dollars to get less and less of the commodities produced. I imagine that his prognostication as to the stabilization of prices under decontrol was fondly accepted by the Conservative party as well as by many members of the Liberal party just a year or two ago, but he was away off the beam there too.
This evening I intend to quote from a succession of clippings which give the views of the people I represent. I do not feel that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association is particularly interested in my point of view or that it would support the things that I stand for, but I do not support the things that it officially stands for. For example, some time ago the association lobbied us with some briefs dealing with prices. This was a statement of the executive council of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association dated November 26,

1947, in regard to the recently announced dominion government policies. It says in part:
These new measures are renewing the public questioning as to the cause of rising prices and who is to blame for them. The greatest factor in prices is wages . . .
That is what the Canadian Manufacturers' Association has to say. However, I find that in direct contradiction of that statement no less a person than R. C. Vaughan, chairman and president of the Canadian National Railways, is quoted in the January-February issue of the Canadian National Magazine. He gives the percentages of increase of the cost of various commodities which enter into the expenses of operation of the Canadian National Railways for 1947 over 1939. General materials show an increase of 75 per cent in eight years; steel, 50-6 per cent; rails, 50-2 per cent, and fuel, 125 per cent. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) will be interested to know that track ties have gone up 121-4 per cent, while other forest products have increased 225 per cent. Labour has increased only 44 per cent during that time.

Mr. Abbott did not announce details of the ceilings but said that "this will mean that Canadian wholesale and retail prices for pork products will be considerably above those prevailing a month ago, but less than many of the prices which have been reported during the past two weeks.
My constituents were not asking for ceilings above those that we had two months ago. The article continues:

The citizens of this country who have followed events sufficiently to pass comment on them have made representations to all members of the House of Commons, some of which I wish to put on the record. This is one from the Canadian Congress of Labour, dated December 12, 1947, addressed to all members of the House of Commons:
Dear Sir:
As a member of parliament, and as a Canadian citizen you are no doubt very seriously concerned with the present upward trend of prices. Conditions have now reached a point where a large proportion of our membership of 369,006 workers are being forced to curtail their purchases of food and other essentials to meet their family budget. This condition applies to your constituents, many of whom are probably members of our organization, as to all other Canadians.
For many months now, Our organization has been repeatedly' urging the government to take action to check increasing living costs and protect living standards. Our representations have been completely ignored, and the government has continued a reckless policy of wiping out controls and subsidies, and wiping out with them the hopes which Canadians have had of a better standard of living. As Canadians, our membership is convinced that we are entitled to a better standard of living, and that such a standard is quite within the realms of possibility7.
We strongly urge that you support the following program:
1-Reimposition of price controls. It is essential that prices be stabilized now at a reasonable level.
They go on to suggest the reimposition of the excess profits tax, the removal of the new excise tax on Canadian goods, and raising the income tax exemptions. But nowhere in this brief is there any reference to setting up a parliamentary committee which will have the effect of delaying action. They say:	Give
us action now.
Here is still another one. This is from the United Mine Workers of America, addressed to the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister:
Dear Sir:
When the session of the commons opens early next month your government, in the opinion of this organization, has at least one vital duty to perform. If nothing else is done price controls and consumer subsidies must be restored.
We are perfectly familiar with some of the difficulties involved in using price control and consumer subsidies as barriers to inflation. But these difficulties are no greater than those successfully surmounted during world war II.
As in wartime, so now, the overwhelming majority of the Canadian people demand protection for their already meagre living standards by the use of controlled prices, consumer subsidies and the suppression of profiteering.
Prices Committee

Only an infinitesimal, though admittedly a powerful, section of the nation profits from the present inflationary rise of prices, reduction in real earnings and upsurge of profits.
* Then, because the government was aware that housewives, consumer leagues and other people who are concerned with doing their daily shopping were raising a clamour against the government, it subsidized the Canadian Association of Consumers. Hon. members might expect that this body would be somewhat friendly to the government which had, as it were, set them up in business. This association, on January 20 last, sent to the members of the House of Commons certain recommendations, of which I shall read only the first paragraph. The following recommendations are made:
1. That an immediate emergency program be put into effect at once to halt the inflationary trend, and that this be done in the following ways:
(a)	That selective price controls on essential foods be applied immediately where unreasonable price rises exist; and
(b)	That the embargo on essential nutritional fresh vegetables such as cabbages and carrots, be lifted, and that steps be taken to safeguard the prices at which they will be sold.
There is in my city an association of working people called the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool Employees' Association. They sent to me a copy of a letter which was addressed to the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, Prime Minister, on January 15, 1948, and I shall quote part of this too:
As a group of some 2,090 employees in the province of Saskatchewan, with members in Manitoba and Ontario, we are gravely concerned with the increasing cost of living and its disastrous effect upon the people.
Further on, they say:
We would respectfully suggest the reimposition of the excess profits tax. This suggestion is not idly made with the intention of shifting a burden from one section to another, but we believe that there is a good reason for the reimposition of this tax, inasmuch as it is now apparent a great many of the business people of Canada have blatantly ignored their responsibility to the national welfare and have concerned themselves only with exploiting the situation for their own individual or collective gain. There is the undeniable responsibility on our business leaders to realize that it is not always in the best interests to charge all the traffic will bear. As this factor has been ignored, it appears that the reimposition of the excess profits tax would be the most effective way of bringing these people into line.
Third, if and when it is obvious that commodities are increasing in their cost to the consumer out of all proportion to the production factors involved, it is our opinion that the government should impose price controls.
In answer to my hon. friend who interjected, they do not ask for a committee of parliament to do any investigating.

Greetings:
On April 4, 19413, the executive council of this congress, along with an accompanying delegation, met with the dominion government and stressed the need of the wartime prices and control board being reconstituted to include representatives of labour. Foreseeing the ceasing of controls, we wanted some protection for the consumer. No attention was paid to our request.
On March 28, 1947, we met again with the government. In dealing with the question of price control, we stated:
"We view with alarm the manner in which the government has weakened its effort in the direction of controlling prices. It must be recognized that every rise in costs is a corresponding reduction in the standard of living of most Canadian citizens and while on the one hand we see plenty of evidence of a desire to control labour, we see little or nothing being done in curtailing the activities of business in the direction of excess profits."
In the interests of most Canadian people, we urged our dominion government 'to reconsider the lifting of price controls and return to the able and efficient methods demonstrated in actual operation (during the war periods) to be fully possible and workable.
What the government did on this was ignore the requests of labour and go over "hook, line and sinker" to the side of big business for bigger profits. Since then, we. and very many others, have many times protested the rising prices. No need to fool ourselves. Big business is in the saddle in the department of government that should control prices just as strong as it is in the Department of Transport. The fact that it takes one dollar to buy 50 cents worth of food is not worrying the government. What are we going to do about it? What are you going to do about it? What are we all going to do about it?
I did not read these extracts with the object of killing some moments in this House of Commons. These are letters from the men and women of this country who produce, who toil. They are not coupon clippers, lilies of the field. They work. This is a compendium of opinion of the workers of Canada. I want to say to the Prime Minister with all humility that he is ending a long illustrious career in this House of Commons by flaunting the will of the people who elected him, as they did me, if he does not act now.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to delay unduly the business of the house or the appointment of this urgent and necessary committee. I am aware that most of the speeches delivered in the house are for publicity reasons rather than for the purpose of criticizing the present action of the government.

I shall therefore be brief and be content with placing on record the following resolution which I recently received from the stone-workers of St. Marc. I quote:
Saint Marc, January 19, 1948. Mr. Pierre Gauthier, M.P.,
Sir,
At its last regular meeting held on January 14, it was unanimously resolved by the members of our union to beg that you put before the government our united plea for an immediate check on the startling increase in the cost of living.
We know what an energetic and determined stand you take when upholding the -welfare of your constituents who are now the victims of grave injustice. You are no doubt aware that our association, some 725 strong, whose members are all stone-workers, has signed a joint year-long contract with our employers. As we intend to respect our signature, we must therefore stretch our small earnings to cope with these increases. Needless to say, our families' standard of living is too low. We therefore trust that you will co-operate fully with us in helping us fight this dreadful scourge that is swooping down on our working class.
We hope to congratulate you when your endeavours meet with the success to which we look forward most eagerly.
Yours sincerely.
The Stone Workers' Union
Raymond Dussault, President Herve Naud, Secretary
I am just trying to show our workers that the cause of the delay is not to be found on our side but rather on the opposition side of the house. While I am on my feet, may I make a suggestion to the committee who will be appointed soon, I hope. They should pay special attention to the spread between the prices received by the producers and the prices paid by the consumers. In other words, let them investigate more particularly the difference between the cost of production and the selling price which goes to the middleman. There they may find producers who are asking too much, unscrupulous jobbers and others who are responsible for the increased cost of living. I sincerely hope that the committee will inquire more particularly into the spread between prices paid by the consumer and prices received by the producer.

Mr. Speaker, at the risk of offending a lot of people on the other side of the house who, no doubt, would like to see this measure go through tonight, I consider it incumbent on me to say something on it. There is no doubt that when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) speaks he will castigate the house for wasting time. He will tell the people of the country that we have wasted a week debating the setting up of this committee when the committee might have been doing something with regard to the problem that we are discussing. My answer to that kind of argument is that we have not wasted any time. In my opinion, the time of the house has been spent very' well in the last few days in trying to get the government to accept its responsibility, because it is not the responsibility of any particular committee.
During the short time the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) spoke, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) interjected something, and in case it got on the record I am going to straighten it out. I did not like it. The hon. member for Regina City was quoting from the United Mine Workers of America, and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni interjected, "They are all communists." I resent that remark very much. I am a member of the united mine workers myself and have been for the last thirty years, and
Prices Committee

I draw his attention to the fact that, during the war and after, there were no coal miners picked up for subversive activities. The ones who were picked up for subversive activities and tried for espionage were all government employees and not coal miners. I want to make that clear. The coal miners of the country did a very good job during the war and are still doing it, and I think an interjection of that kind from the hon. member for Comox-Alberni is uncalled for. As a rule he shows pretty good common sense, but tonight I do not think he did in some of the interjections he was chucking across the floor.
Looking at this motion from a common-sense point of view, I do not think there is any necessity for setting up any committee to determine why the cost of living is as it is in Canada today. That should be quite clear to everyone in this house. I remember distinctly my reaction to the first two or three steps that wrecked the price structure in this country and started the spiral of inflation we have today, and those steps were taken by-the government and argued and fought for in this house by government members.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), who was minister of finance at the time I refer to, stated this afternoon that when they allowed the increase in basic steel and the increase in the price of farm machinery there was a lot of discussion and a lot of abuse and recriminations across the floor. That is quite true. I believe that anyone who realized the situation at that time will recognize that these were the steps that were going to set up the condition we have in this country today.
I do not think there is any necessity for setting up a committee to determine what is wrong today. My mind goes back to a time just prior to the 1945 election when the luxury tax of twenty-five per cent was removed and an order issued to the manufacturers of the country making it mandatory to retain the price as it was to the consumer. That was number one. Number two was this. When the steel companies-

The records have it. The second step that was taken was this. The steel companies of the country came and

asked for a $5 a ton increase in basic steel, which meant a $9 a ton increase in fabricated steel. Now steel ramifies all through the economy of the country. We argued against that increase; nevertheless the government permitted it, and in an examination of the balance sheets of the steel companies of Canada before the industrial relations committee, it was proven to us that there was no justification for that increase in basic steel at that time. The steel companies were in a financial position to look after any additional cost that might accrue because of the five or ten cent increase for which the steel workers were looking.
In my opinion, that increase in basic steel set off the spiral of inflation that we have today. You increased the cost in practically all your fabricated materials into which steel enters, and steel is used largely throughout our whole economy. Second, wThen the farm machine companies came in, and they' came in because there was an increase granted in the price of steel, they were granted a 12J per cent increase in the price of farm machinery, and immediately that increased the cost of farm products. That increase entered into the farmer's cost of production and he began looking for a compensating increase in farm commodities.
These are the steps that started the whole mess that we are in today in price increases, and I do not think there is any necessity' for setting up a committee to determine how to get out of that mess. The way to get out of it is the way we got into it. These increases at that time were authorized by the wartime prices and trade board; and in an examination of the balance sheets of the farm machine companies and the steel companies, and a questioning of Mr. Donald Gordon in the reconstruction committee, it was proved to the satisfaction of every member of the committee that there was no justification for the increase. And' there was no examination of the books of either the steel companies or the farm machine companies before the increases were granted.
That is what started the whole business, with the result that we have the upward trend we see today. The Minister of Justice this afternoon tried to justify the position the government is now taking by pointing out that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) had suggested that a. factfinding committee should be set up for the purpose of easing the mind of the public and finding out what the actual situation was and so forth. He pointed out also that the hon. member for Calgary' West (Mr. Smith), in another emergency, in the steel strike, had

Prices Committee
suggested1 the setting up of a committee. I would point out to the government and to the Minister of Justice that the same group advocated the removal of controls, the removal of subsidies, and getting back to free enterprise, and I believe that most of the trouble over there today is, that too much Tory advice has been taken. In my opinion, there is no solution in this committee.
The committee on industrial relations was set up at the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary West and I was a member of that committee. I went into the committee fully intending to do something and I think something could have been done, but when you got into the committee you found yourself on the outside looking in-a government-dominated committee. Motions were made; suggestions were offered that would have cured the situation we were confronted with at that time, but none of them was taken. It was pointed out to us definitely that that committee had no legal status and could not recommend anything that might mean an expenditure of money. That committee could Dot do anything and it came back and reported nothing. Evidence was taken; the recommendations made were shelved, and the matter was settled later by ordeF in council.
To go into another committee on this particular matter is something I am not very much concerned about. In my opinion, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) this afternoon talked common sense and was honest in trying to get something done. I believe he honestly meant that something should be done, and it is just too bad that there were not more men on that side of the house who took the same position.
My conception of this whole situation, and of many other things we have discussed in this house, is that there is no honest will to do something. There is not one of these things that could not be headed off, checked, cured and fixed up if we really wanted to do it. If we honestly went after the problem and applied the authority that this House of Commons has in a given situation that may arise in this country it could be cured, and this is one such situation. There is no reason in the world why this house cannot cure the situation at the present time.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) yesterday made a statement at which I was amazed, in the face of what we have now, with demands from all over the country, with the labour unrest that prevails, with the two congresses of labour preparing new wage demands, which can mean new stoppages of work across the country and all the rest of it.
The Minister of National Revenue rose in his place yesterday, in answer to the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) and said, "Yes, we are holding the compulsory savings portion of the income tax and are applying it to back taxes that may have accrued."

Just a minute and I will
tell you why I was surprised. You have now reached the point where you are going to pay that money out anyway. That is point number one. Point number two is this. While you had that money, there was two per cent interest accruing on it. But eight per cent interest is charged on back taxes. So that, instead of paying the money out now, when you are legitimately entitled to pay it out, you are holding it. The man who owns it got two per cent, and you are going to extract eight per cent as a penalty because of back taxes. That is why I was amazed at it. When people were in distress, and when they wanted to apply that tax to liquidate any indebtedness they had to the department, you were not going to pay it out then. You were still holding it. You were still using it. It was quite all right. You were not concerned about the circumstances or condition of a person who had to enter hospital, for example, to undergo a serious operation. Many pleas were made along those lines, where there were extenuating circumstances, asking if it could not be paid. In my opinion, the government are today taking six per cent interest out of the compulsory savings which legitimately belong to the taxpayer, while they gave him only two per cent interest on the money. Perhaps the minister or the experts behind the scenes never really thought about this. But do not forget that the man in the street will think about it, because that struck me in the face as soon as the minister made that statement. I see it as a means of getting, by a back-door move, six per cent of the money that belongs to somebody else, and I do not think it does any credit to anyone in the department who may have had that brain wave.

I will explain why I am so greatly interested in that. In the Nova Scotia mining industry within the last few months some fifteen hundred miners, sixty-five years of age, were laid off, with pensions ranging from $16 a month to about $30. Many of these miners have an indebtedness in back taxes as a result of the methods used in deducting taxes at the source. There is ten per cent or fifteen per cent of a backlog andl it accumulates. With regard to many of these men, when they got their first pension cheque of $15, $20 or $25, the first thing that was taken off them was $4, $5 or $6 for back income tax. Many of them have these compulsory savings. Prior to coming here, I talked to many of them, and I have also written to the minister on the subject asking if there was not a possibility of having those back taxes waived. After forty years in an industry, breaking your back, without any pension

or anything whatsoever-despite the fact that they fought for many years and tried to get some kind of superannuation arrangement but were not successful-to find yourself in the position of being chucked in the street is a most unfortunate thing. For sympathetic reasons, if for no others, I think the minister might consider the proposition of making it as easy as possible for the men who find themselves in that position, with regard to the collection of back taxes accumulated because of the system of collecting taxes and through no fault of their own. Mr. Bracken:	Mr. Speaker, in view of
the proposed change by the Prime Minister, I should' like to ask if, in view of the fact that the debate on the speech from the throne will not go on tomorrow, therefore, under the original plan only one day this week will be allowed for that debate. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

I may say quite frankly that, after the heat shown by the Prime Minister at three o'clock this afternoon with respect to the program since this house met ten days ago, I have no intention whatever of proposing what work should be done tomorrow.
The understanding at the beginning, the program advanced by the Prime Minister, was that three days a week would be devoted to government business and two days to the speech from the throne. On Tuesday evening, when the next two days had been set aside by himself for discussing the speech from the throne, he came over here and asked if it was agreeable to go on with this measure on Wednesday. As he said himself tonight, that was accepted. That was his wish. There was no suggestion as to what should be done after Wednesday.
I do not question what the Prime Minister hoped for, and I am not criticizing what was done. But in view of the attitude taken by
the Prime Minister at three o'clock this afternoon, in which he criticized the opposition because somebody had raised a point of order -properly raised, I think; we did not raise it, but it was properly raised; then we were censured-I do not propose to put myself in that position again. Whatever the Prime Minister wishes to do tomorrow, I leave it to the government. He can announce it, and we will follow it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

Mr. Speaker, I have been in this house for a good many years, and I think I am pretty well known to all members of the house. I think I can say that if anyone will give his expression of view honestly he will have to admit that I have done my best to try to have the work of this house carried on with as much in the way of co-operation as possible between both sides.
I intend to hold to that.
But it takes two to co-operate. And if, when I agree with the opposition that I will give precedence to certain measures at their request, and then I am told later that I am violating some understanding or agreement when I try to continue what has been requested, it becomes difficult indeed to proceed.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: There was no suggestion from here that you were violating anything.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
The trouble with this House of Commons is that we have three parties sitting opposite. When one agrees, one of the others does not agree; and it is a very difficult situation. My view is that we ought to have a government and an opposition, and those who are not for us ought to be against us. I wish everybody on the other side would just constitute themselves one opposition, and allow the government to go on with its business, instead of having three oppositions taking different views on different questions which come up; then, as soon as one comes to an understanding, the other taking; exception to it and saying they have not come' to that understanding.
May I say about this effort to say that there was heat on the part of the Prime Minister today, that it is very easy to put that sort of thing in Hansard. I have not any worry about what my hon. friend wishes to say. Hon. members opposite cannot say more now than they have said against me in the years which have passed. If they like to have Hansard record these expressions, well and good. Let them make them, and the country can judge whether or not I have tried to do my duty in this house.
I wish to point this fact out to hon. gentlemen opposite that if I were to say tonight that tomorrow we will go on with the debate
Business oj the Howe

on the address, which I presume will be said is what we ought to have done, it would be pointed out that the leader of the opposition had said:
If vre proceed now, as he suggests, will he be willing .to continue the debate on the speech from the throne on Friday as well as on Thursday?
To which I replied:
I would see no objection to that.
I am prepared to go on with the debate on the address tomorrow. But I wish hon. gentlemen opposite to answer this question if they will: What about Monday? Am I to hold to what I said to the house at the beginning? If we have three days a week on the emergency measufes and two days on the address, what is to become of this motion? It has had the precedence it had in order to oblige hon. gentlemen opposite.
I see this kind of situation arise, and it cannot be solved in any way other than by co-operation between the different parties in the house. That kind of co-operation is arranged in the old country between the whips. In the old country, at Westminster, they adopt the policy of setting aside a certain number of days, and try to close up a debate within that time. Hon. gentlemen opposite could follow that splendid example. I think if they do we shall make headway with the work of parliament. But if they do not, I cannot see how the business is to be conducted from week to week in other than a fashion in which no one can say what will take place from one day to another.
In order not to have it said that I am blocking any undertaking in regard to Friday, I will say now that the business for tomorrow will be the debate on the address. When Monday comes I should hope hon. gentlemen opposite will agree to continue with this debate on the motion to set up the committee. But it requires unanimous consent of the house; and if that unanimous consent is not given we shall have to continue with emergency measures until we reach a time when we can get unanimous consent.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Perhaps the lecture we have just been read was the result of a question on the point of order which I raised this afternoon. If the Prime Minister had been as considerate of the house yesterday at six o'clock as he has been tonight, that question would never have arisen. If he had said last night, "Now, I propose to continue tomorrow with the debate on this motion to set up a committee; I presume that will be all right for members on the opposition side", I am satisfied everyone would have given the Prime Minister every

co-operation. Now he thinks we are in a position to read his mind, and that was said this afternoon.
I want the Prime Minister to understand that any reasonable person reading what he said to the leader of the opposition the other day with regard to procedure, and the priority of this particular job in which we have been engaged for several days, could not possibly determine whether that was to continue today, in spite of the printed routine proceedings on the order paper. I challenge anyone, who has an unbiased view, to pick it up and look it over, and also to look over Hansard, and to answer it any better than I answered it.
I want it definitely known that the only reason I rose to a point of order this afternoon was to secure and to preserve the rights of members in this house

and for no other reason. I want to say that nobody has given the government more co-operation by way of agreement-and stayed with it-than we have. I will go further and say that whenever a reasonable request is made of members on this side of the house by the Prime Minister or the government in order to facilitate the business of the house, he will find me and my group ready to co-operate with him. But we want it definitely known that he has to make a request, and has to make it, not in a testy manner, but in a pleasant manner.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
I do not wish to continue this discussion unnecessarily, but my hon. friend has said two things tonight to which I must refer. He said if I had been as considerate last night as I am tonight that there would have been no occasion for any difficulty. Then he began his remarks tonight by saying that I had been reading a lecture to the house. That is not being considerate. I must say that I am anxious in every way to be as considerate to all sides of the house as possible. I never for one moment thought there would be the slightest exception taken to going on with the debate on this motion to set up a committee. The whole purpose of giving precedence to that motion was that we might get through with it as quickly as possible.
Looking tonight at what I said last night, I find that the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Matthews) who was speaking said:
May I, Mr. Speaker, have the privilege of moving the adjournment of the debate.
And then:
Mr. Mackenzie King: We shall continue this debate tomorrow.
I cannot see wherein that was not treating the house with courtesy. My duty is, as the

Business oj the House
leader of the opposition said tonight, to indicate the business for tomorrow. I indicated it. If hon. gentlemen wish to co-operate they will find that I am doing everything in my power-indeed I will go beyond what the ordinary person would expect-in trying to make arrangements which will be satisfactory. But if they are determined to misconstrue everything I say, I shall have to allow matters to take the best course that they can take.
But I will say to hon. members that there is a heavy program ahead of parliament at this session. I think hon. members will find it to their advantage to endeavour to co-operate as much as they can with each other and with the different parties in the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
May I just say a word
on behalf of our group. I do not intend to participate in the disputes that have arisen, but I want to say a word about the business of the house tomorrow. By virtue of the motion passed last Monday, the order paper tomorrow will have government orders first. So far as we are concerned, if the government prefers to go ahead with the government order of its choice, namely, the motion we have been discussing today, that will be quite satisfactory to us. If the Prime Minister decides that we go on to debate the address in reply, that is all right with us, but we are not asking for it.
When Monday comes, again by reason of the motion passed last Monday the order
paper will have government orders first and there will be no problem. No unanimous consent will be required. If today's motion has not been completed the government can call it and we can go on with it then.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
So far as the Prime
Minister's announcement about tomorrow's business is concerned, that is quite acceptable. As to Monday, I wish to assure him that there will be no objection on this side of the house if he proceeds, as he suggests, with the measure that was being discussed today.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
There could not be any
objection.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Whether there could or
could not, we will raise none. I would say this one other thing. The Prime Minister has given us tonight what someone has referred to as a lecture. I refused to take the responsibility for tomorrow's work only because of the comment which he directed to this party at three o'clock. We had raised no objection to the procedure, but the Prime Minister said that if a certain attitude was to be adopted he would not be prepared to co-operate, or words to that effect. That is the reason why I answered the Prime Minister as I did tonight.
Mr, GILLIS: Is there any reason why we could not go on with this motion tomorrow?
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 11.15 p.m.

Friday, February 6, 1948
